what: `glytdbud-expense` for the special revenue funds
why: NARROWED 5 October 2026 for the SCHOOL funds in FY2024. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (`sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/`, see its PROVENANCE note) include the school department's FY2024 period 13 `glytdbud` report covering every school fund, grants and revolving funds included, at org and object level. The town's own special revenue funds are not in it. The identical report the town already runs for the general fund and for each of the four enterprise funds, pointed at funds 13xx/22xx/26xx–29xx instead. — closes: Turns **every restricted edge** above from presumption into traced fact — athletics, lunch, circuit breaker, extended day, and every grant.

what: WRRS annual actuarial valuation, by member unit
why: Published by the retirement system. — closes: Sizes the school share of the $2.39M pension assessment.

what: The Town Manager’s revenue apportionment worksheet
why: Seen once; we do not hold it. — closes: Documents the convention by which general-fund revenue is presented as split across departments. It cannot make the edge traceable — nothing can — but it makes the convention citable.

what: DESE End of Year Financial Report
why: NARROWED 5 October 2026. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (`sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/`, see its PROVENANCE note) include the district's FY2023 and FY2024 End of Year Financial Report WORKBOOKS (`eoy23` and `eoy24`, district 162, Schedules 1, 3, 18, 19 and 20), which separate spending by fund. Both are working copies passed on from a Select Board member's records request, not the reports as filed: the FY24 grant columns do not match DESE's published file. The filed reports remain the remedy. Published by the state. — closes: Separates district spending by FUND, which is the one thing the town’s budget documents never show.

what: Where bus fee receipts are booked
why: A revenue account, a fund, or a statement that they are netted before booking. — closes: The fee schedule is published and verified; `STUDENTBUS` shows zero. **A charged fee with no observable destination** is the clearest single gap in this model.

what: The period 13 ledger
why: The year-end close. — closes: Reconciles FY2026 properly; period 12 is used for now.

what: How many people the schools actually employ
why: The town publishes per-school staff ROSTERS in every annual report, FY2011 to FY2025 — a list of names. A roster carries **no FTE**, so a 0.4 music teacher and a full-timer are one row each, and it is a point in time, undated within the year. A count of names the town printed is a real quantity and it is **not a staffing level**. AND THE DISTRICT’S OWN CONTACT SHEETS DO NOT AGREE WITH EACH OTHER, which this project did not know until it held them: its roll-up of every employee names 257 people, the five listings the office and the four schools keep name 45 the roll-up does not, and the roll-up names people no building lists — Primary leaves its own paraprofessionals off the sheet the school keeps. Some of that difference is one person written two ways (`Skye Abreu` on one, `Skye Abrue` on the other) and nothing published distinguishes a second spelling from a second person, because no sheet carries an employee identifier. So there is no count of district staff here that two documents support. — closes: a staffing report stating FTE by position and year.

what: Which fund pays which post
why: This is the load-bearing one. The rosters name people and the budget names dollars, and **nothing published joins them to a funding source**. So a paraprofessional line rising cannot be distinguished from a grant that was paying for those posts ending — which is exactly what the special education escalator rests on. — closes: DESE's End of Year Financial Report, which separates spending by fund.

what: Whether a budgeted position was filled
why: A budget line is money the town has to raise, not a person in a chair. A line funded all year for a post vacant half of it looks identical on the page to one that was filled. **Bounded, not settled**: the rosters show who was printed, which narrows the question without answering it. — closes: a filled-position list, or payroll by position rather than by name.

what: School share of the town’s health insurance before FY2026
why: The town’s insurance department prints one undivided `Health Insurance CH 32B` line in fifteen of the sixteen annual reports · a school share is named only in the FY2023 report and in the FY2026 ledger, so no year between them can be split. — closes: The town’s Chapter 32B enrollment schedule, which counts insured employees and retirees by department and would split every year rather than the two that happened to be printed.

what: School share of Medicare, active health insurance and the insurance reserves
why: Five of the seven FY2026 insurance accounts — active health insurance, Medicare, life insurance, insurance cost control and Public Employee Committee expenses — carry nothing in their names that says which side of the town they are for, so the school portion of them is not separable in any year. — closes: The town’s Chapter 32B enrollment schedule, which counts insured employees and retirees by department.

what: The town’s Chapter 32B enrollment schedule
why: NARROWED 5 October 2026. The Finance Committee's general fund history (FY2010-FY2025, sources/data/gl-history.csv) carries a separate SCHOOL RETIREES health insurance line in the town's budget in every year FY2022-FY2025, original budget 1,149,925 rising to 1,411,181 -- so the RETIREE split is printed in four years, not two. The split of active employees' insurance between town and schools is still not printed. Not published anywhere in this archive; the town must hold one to administer the plan and set premium shares. — closes: Splits every insurance account between the town and the schools, in every year, instead of in the two years the split happens to be printed.

what: What the four `ADJ EXP` journal entries moved, and from where
why: $254,121.18 — 65% of everything that reached the athletics revolving fund in FY2025 — arrived on four general-journal entries whose entire description is an expense adjustment made per a memo. An entry raising cash in a fund and labelled as an expense adjustment fits at least three readings: expenses charged here and later moved elsewhere, a transfer in from another fund, or a correction of charges posted to the wrong account. Those are different facts about the world and identical facts on the page, and the same shape of entry could be adjusting any fund in the town without either budget document showing a trace. — closes: the five memos the ledger names, dated 08/12/24, 01/30/25, 05/02/25, 07/02/25 and 08/20/2025.

what: Whether a general fund athletics line is net of the revolving fund
why: In FY2024 the town’s comparable athletics lines came to $124,301 against $351,643 the district’s own sport-by-sport workbook totals for the same categories — so the appropriation covered 35% of the cost. That is measurable for FY2024 and FY2025 only, because those are the only years anybody published both halves. For every other year, and every other programme, a line that rose because the cost rose looks exactly like a line that rose because a fund stopped paying part of it. — closes: the MUNIS `Account_Detail` export for the general fund athletics orgs S3066672 and S3066671, all object codes.

what: How many children play sports
why: Two town documents give 593 and 649 for the same year and count different things: one counts fee categories, the other counts participations by sport, and a participation is not a child — one student playing three seasons is three of them. Some workbook rows are negative, subtracting out-of-district athletes back out, so a season total is a net figure rather than a headcount of bodies. Nothing published is an unduplicated count. — closes: an unduplicated athlete roster, or a participation report that states whether it counts students or participations.

what: What the $87,293.86 is that the FY2023 annual report states twice and differently
why: Two tables printed in the same FY2023 annual town report state the money held in special revenue and enterprise funds, and they disagree. The combined balance sheet on printed page 24 gives TOTAL FUND EQUITY of $6,131,303.68 for SPECIAL REVENUE and $3,812,502.24 for ENTERPRISE, $9,943,805.92 together. The special revenue schedule in the same report prints a GRAND TOTAL carried forward of $10,031,099.78. The difference is $87,293.86, where FY2011, FY2013, FY2019 and FY2022 agree to the cent. It is not a misreading: the FY2023 page was transcribed and every column foots to its own printed TOTAL ASSETS, TOTAL LIABILITIES and TOTAL FUND EQUITY, the accounting identity holds in all six columns, and the long-term debt mirror agrees. So FY2023 is transcribed and deliberately NOT written into the dataset, which is why the combined balance sheet here stops at FY2022 while the special revenue schedule runs to FY2023. One explanation has been tested and RULED OUT: the fund 'Sale of Cemetery Lots' carried $87,308.09 in FY2023, within $14.23 of the gap, which suggested a fund counted in one statement and classified elsewhere in the other. It is not that — the same fund appears in the schedule in all thirteen years including the four where the two documents agree to the cent, so it is counted consistently and the near-match is a coincidence. What the difference IS remains unestablished; nothing here says which document is right, nor whether it is connected to the $17,861.24 of grant funds the town restated between the FY2022 and FY2023 reports. Those are two different amounts and nothing joins them. — closes: the Town's FY2023 trial balance or general ledger fund balances as of 30 June 2023, which would say which of its own two published tables the accounting system agrees with.

what: The Cherry Sheet itself — what the state told Lunenburg to expect, receipt by receipt
why: This archive holds no Cherry Sheet for any year. The Cherry Sheet is the state’s own statement of estimated aid and assessments to a Massachusetts town, and it is what a tax rate is set on. Without it the only measurement of aid estimate error this project can make is one net line on the Division of Local Services free cash proof — `Excess/Shortfall Cherry Sheet Receipts (CL#8)` — which lumps Chapter 70, Unrestricted General Government Aid, the abatement reimbursements and every other receipt into a single figure. So a year that came in $390,814 short can be reported as short and cannot be reported as short in anything. — closes: DLS Cherry Sheet CS 1-ER (estimated receipts) and CS 1-EB (estimated charges) for Lunenburg, FY2021 to FY2027.

what: Whether a shortfall in state aid falls on the schools or on the rest of the town
why: Chapter 70 is 35% of the school appropriation and the town has no vote on it, so which side of the budget absorbs a miss is the question a resident actually has. Nothing published answers it. The free cash proof states one net cherry sheet figure for the whole town; the general ledger’s state aid accounts share no organisation code with any expense account, 0 of 222, so no aid dollar can be followed to anything it paid for; and the appropriation is voted before the final aid number is known. A year where aid rose and the appropriation rose with it and a year where aid was flat and the town covered the difference are different facts about the world and identical facts on the page. — closes: the Town’s FY-end recap (Form A-1) beside the Cherry Sheet for the same year, which states estimated and actual receipts on one page.

what: How many children Chapter 70 is actually paid for
why: The aid is calculated on a `Foundation enrollment` of 1,599 in DESE’s FY27 Chapter 70 summary. DESE publishes three other counts for the same district — Student Headcount, In-District FTE Pupils and Total FTE Pupils — and in the latest year published they are 1,563, 1,568.9 and 1,665.9. Four numbers, one agency, none of them equal, measured on different dates and counting different things. So every per-pupil figure on this project, including aid per pupil, is a division by a count whose definition has to be stated with it, and no published document reconciles the foundation count to the children in the buildings. — closes: DESE’s FY27 foundation enrollment worksheet for Lunenburg, which states the October 1 count by grade and category the formula was run on.

what: Why DLS certifies a different amount from the free cash its own proof identifies
why: The Division of Local Services’ free cash proof cross-foots exactly: in all 45 town-years of the nine-town set the eleven component lines sum, to the cent, to the workbook’s own `Identified Free Cash July 1,`. But that is **not the figure DLS certifies**. `Current Year Calculation` — the number the Town quotes, the number the Finance Director announced, and the number that carries into the next year — differs from it in all 45, by $361,912 for Lunenburg in 2025 and by 69% for Uxbridge in 2024. The workbook prints no reconciling line, and nothing in this archive states what the adjustment is. — closes: DLS’s free cash certification letter to the Town, which states the adjustments made between the balance sheet the Town submitted and the amount certified.

what: Which departments’ unspent appropriations produced the free cash
why: Money appropriated and not spent is the largest single component of Lunenburg’s free cash — 47% of five years of it, and 66% of the record 2025 certification. It is published as **one town-wide figure** across 67 departments. Prudence, a post left vacant, a project that slipped into the next year and a line that was over-budgeted from the start are four different facts about the world and one number on the page. — closes: the period 13 general ledger, showing budget, expended and turnback for each department at the year-end close.

what: How much of free cash is the schools’
why: Free cash is certified for the town as a whole. Neither the DLS proof nor the Town’s own undesignated fund balance roll-forward attributes any component to any department, so **nothing published says how much of it the school department’s unspent appropriation produced** — nor how much of any appropriation of it reaches the schools. The projection on this site is built from budget columns and free cash is derived from actuals; they are subtracted once, side by side, and never joined. — closes: a departmental turnback schedule for the year-end close, which would split the unexpended appropriations line by department.

what: Whether Lunenburg’s free cash is unusual for a town its size
why: The DLS proof carries **no denominator** — no population, budget, revenue or levy for any of the nine towns, Lunenburg included. So Littleton’s $11.3M against Shirley’s $272K says nothing about which is closer to its own target, and free cash as a share of the operating budget cannot be computed for a peer at all. Composition and volatility are ratios and do compare; the level does not, and is not shown. — closes: the Tax Rate Recapitulation (Schedule A) for each town, which prints the operating budget the ratio needs.

what: Why the Town’s undesignated fund balance and DLS’s free cash differ
why: Two publishers describe the same 30 June balance sheet and print three different figures. The Town’s annual report roll-forward gives an undesignated fund balance of $4,236,488.24 at 30 June 2025; DLS identifies $3,716,282 of free cash on the same date and certifies $3,354,370. **Each worksheet cross-foots exactly to its own printed total**, and the FY2024 report’s closing balance is the FY2025 report’s opening one to the cent — so neither is in error, and no document in this archive prints a line between any pair of the three. — closes: the Town’s free cash submission to DLS (the balance sheet and the reconciliation of receivables and deferred revenue that accompanies it).

what: What the $102,000.00 is that the FY2024 enterprise balance sheet classifies two ways at once
why: The Combining Balance Sheet - Enterprise Funds in the FY2024 annual town report — printed twice, on printed pages 21 and 28, identically — prints 'Reserved for expenditures' as 400,000.00 in the Sewer column and 502,000.00 in the Totals (Memorandum Only) column, and prints 'Unreserved retained earnings' as 2,973,842.15 in the memorandum column where the four fund columns (1,813,817.53 Sewer, 51,333.93 Water, 181,853.82 Solid Waste, 1,028,836.87 PEG Access) add to 3,075,842.15. The memorandum column is $102,000.00 high on the first line and $102,000.00 low on the second, so the two cancel and Total Fund Equity (3,483,633.65), Total Assets, the identity and the sheet's own printed PROOF row all still tie in every column — compensating errors, invisible to any check that reads only totals. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which presentation is right, or what the $102,000.00 is. A reservation sitting in a fund column that prints blank, a memorandum column keyed to a different worksheet row, and a reclassification made only in the total column all fit the same signature, and nothing on the page distinguishes them. These are ratepayer funds; nothing here is general-fund money. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2024 trial balance for the enterprise funds, which would state the reserved and unreserved balance of each fund separately.

what: What the town held town-wide at 30 June 2024 and 30 June 2025
why: The FY2024 and FY2025 annual town reports print NO combined balance sheet across all fund types and account groups — the schedule the reports carried every year from FY2011 to FY2023. In both editions the table of contents lists 'Balance Sheet for FY Ending June 30, 2024' at Page 21 and 'Balance Sheet for FY Ending June 30, 2025' at Page 21 respectively, and printed page 21 of each holds the Combining Balance Sheet - Enterprise Funds instead; FY2024 prints that enterprise sheet a second time on page 28, which is where its contents page says it should be. So for two consecutive years the only balance sheet the town published covers four ratepayer enterprise funds and says nothing about the general fund, special revenue, capital projects, trust and agency, or long-term debt. The consequence is that the general fund's cash, receivables, reserves and undesignated fund balance — the figures free cash is built out of — cannot be read for either year, and the balance_sheet dataset stops at FY2023 for that reason rather than by choice. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the town-wide sheet was produced and dropped in layout or never produced; nothing in either report says. — closes: the Town Accountant's year-end balance sheet submitted to the Division of Local Services for FY2024 and FY2025, or the town's audited financial statements for those years.

what: What the PEG Access enterprise fund actually held at 30 June 2025
why: Three figures for the same fund on the same date appear in the same FY2025 annual town report and no document in this archive prints a line between any two of them. The PAC report's FY25 REVENUE vs EXPENSES table (printed page 60, pdf 64) gives an Ending Balance of $30,632, computed on its own face as Beginning Balance $208,772 less Expenses $178,140 -- and the prose beside it says the $208,772 was "the budget starting balance", so the ending balance is unspent spending authority rather than money. The Treasurer's Cash schedule in the same report prints `Bartholomew- PEG Access Enterprise Fund 782,591.31$`. The Combining Balance Sheet - Enterprise Funds (printed page 21, pdf 25) prints PEG Access Total Fund Equity of $1,072,661.74, against $1,028,836.87 the year before -- a rise of $43,824.87, where the statement's own revenue less expenses is $262,565 - $178,140 = $84,425. The two do not reconcile and nothing on either page relates them. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which quantity any of the three is; a budget balance, a bank balance and a fund equity are three different things and the report labels none of them as such. -- closes: the Town Accountant's FY2025 year-end statement of revenues, expenditures and changes in fund balance for the PEG Access and Cable Related Enterprise Fund, which the annual report does not contain.

what: What the PEG Access fund spent in FY2020 and in FY2024
why: In both years the annual town report prints two totals for the same year's PEG expenses and they differ. FY2020, both tables on printed page 75: `FY20 Line Item Expenses by Percentage` foots to Total $116,933.22 and `FY20 REVENUE vs EXPENSES` prints Expenses $116,933.54 -- 32 cents apart. FY2024: the statement on printed page 63 prints Expenses $174,150 and the line-item table on printed page 64 foots to Total $174,151.16, and since that statement is printed in whole dollars throughout, rounding 174,151.16 gives 174,151 rather than 174,150. Each table foots to its own printed total exactly, so neither is internally wrong; they disagree with each other. FY2017 is a third case of the same shape: its ten printed expense lines add to $74,665.74 against a printed TOTAL of $74,215.73, a difference of $450.01, of which $450.00 is the `Vendor Expenses` line that the facing pie chart also omits. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which figure is the year's expenditure in any of the three years. -- closes: the MUNIS year-to-date expense report (glytdbud) for the PEG Access and Cable Related Enterprise Fund for FY2017, FY2020 and FY2024, the same report the town already runs for the general fund.

what: Where the PEG Access balance went between FY2019 and FY2021
why: The fund's carried balance is continuous in the report from FY2015 to FY2019 -- each edition's Starting Balance is the previous edition's Ending Balance to the cent -- and then stops being a series. FY2019 prints a Total of $573,837.37 (starting balance, plus revenue, less expenses, plus the Comcast Tech Fund of $124,796.01); FY2020 opens at $447,813.36, $126,024.01 lower; FY2021 opens at $272,000.00, which the same page's prose states is the budget rather than a balance. One document explains part of it: Article 16 of the FY2019 Annual Town Meeting established a PEG Access Enterprise Fund under MGL c.44 s53F1/2 and transferred into it the balances of the PEG Access and Cable Related Receipts Reserved For Appropriation Fund and the Comcast Tech Capital Grant Fund as of 30 June 2019. So the fund changed legal form at exactly this point, which is why the statement changes shape. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: the amounts transferred, and therefore whether the $126,024.01 step is the transfer, a closing entry, a restatement, or something else. There is also a smaller unexplained step earlier, FY2017's Ending Balance $303,909.77 against FY2018's Starting Balance $303,551.54, $358.23 apart, with no fund change to account for it. -- closes: the Town Accountant's opening and closing trial balances for the PEG Access and Cable Related funds for FY2018, FY2019 and FY2020, showing the transfers in and out.

what: What quantity the Town’s own published state-aid growth rates of 5.3% and 1.4% measure
why: The FY2027 Town Meeting booklet states that "From FY13-FY23 state aid increased at an annual rate of 5.3%, but in the last four years, it has slowed to approximately 1.4%" (3765-town-meeting-booklet-including-warrant, line 338), and does not say which figure it grew. Rebuilding the Town’s own `Subtotal State Aid` line from its own revenue/expenditure worksheets — 23 consecutive budget years, FY2005 to FY2027, notes/findings/state-aid-budget-series.csv — gives 4.5660% for FY2013→FY2023 and 1.9144% for FY2023→FY2027. Neither published rate is reproducible from the Town’s own published series, so a rate quoted to Town Meeting cannot be checked against anything. — closes: the Cherry Sheets themselves (DLS form CS 1-ER for Lunenburg, one per year), or the Town Manager’s working file behind the FY2027 booklet’s revenue narrative.

what: How much of the FY2027 enacted state-aid increase is receipts and how much is offsetting assessments
why: model/finance.py grows a FY2027 base of $11,404,917 + $471,121. The first is the Governor’s GROSS cherry sheet Total Receipts, printed by the FY2027 Town Meeting booklet. The second is recorded in fy27-and-the-override.md as NET — "+$471,121 net (Ch.70, charter/choice receiving tuition, Smart Growth, UGGA, vets/elderly exemptions; offset by higher charter assessments)". A gross figure and a net figure are being added, so the gross FY2027 receipt estimate the projection actually grows is not established, and neither is how much of the increase the Town keeps. This archive holds no Cherry Sheet for any year, which is the only document that prints receipts and assessments side by side. — closes: the FY2027 Cherry Sheet for Lunenburg on the enacted budget (DLS form CS 1-ER), which states each receipt and each assessment separately.

what: What the schools actually spent, per line, in any year before FY2026
why: NARROWED 5 October 2026. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (`sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/`, see its PROVENANCE note) include the school department's FY2024 MUNIS year-to-date report at PERIOD 13 (`glytdbud`, `FOR 2024 13`, generated 08/07/2024, every school fund), which answers FY2024 by ledger, and a general fund budget-vs-actual history, FY2010-FY2025 by account, assembled from MUNIS into one workbook. FY2025 in that workbook is part-year. The district publishes a column headed ACTUAL in its forward budget books, and twelve years of it load as `budget_figure` where stage='restated' — the stage was called `actual` until 7 September 2026, and the rename is the point. Those are RESTATEMENTS — a prior year re-presented inside a document written by the party that spent it — and `document-basis.csv` classifies all sixteen source documents behind them as `restatement` (14) or `forward` (2). None is a ledger. The archive holds ten ledger documents in total, and the only ones reaching school general-fund spending are one quarter of FY23 and FY2026 period 12. So the question 'did the schools spend what they budgeted' cannot be settled before FY2026 from anything published: both sides of the comparison come out of the same budget book, and a restatement cannot show money moved between lines mid-year because approved transfers do not appear in a budget document. — closes: the MUNIS year-end expense report (glytdbud, period 13) for the school department for each year wanted, which is the same report we already hold for FY2026.

what: What the children who leave the district cost, as against how many there are
why: The COUNTS are published and this project now holds them: DESE’s enrollment of town residents by district (dataset vxt3-k35x) states, for every school year from SY2014 to SY2026, how many Lunenburg residents attend each other district and under which programme. SY2026: 58 children under School Choice, 22 at charter schools and 97 at Montachusett Regional as members rather than by choice. The companion file (8xyg-59b2) counts the children arriving the other way, 11 in SY2026. So "a fall in enrollment is not a count of departures" is no longer a reason to refuse the question — the departures are counted. What is NOT published anywhere in this archive is the MONEY: not one document states the tuition Lunenburg is assessed for those 58 children, or for the 22 at charters, and the two rates are set differently and are higher for special education. — closes: DLS Cherry Sheet CS 1-EB (estimated charges) for Lunenburg, which prints the school choice sending and charter tuition assessments on their own lines.

what: Which TABLE in a document is ledger-backed, rather than which document is
why: `document-basis.csv` carries one basis per document — 322 paths, 322 rows — and that granularity is wrong for the annual town reports, which are the source of a great deal of what this project publishes. The FY2022 annual town report is classified `forward`, and it contains both 'Combined balance sheet, all fund types and account groups, 30 June 2022' and 'FY 2023 Omnibus Budget (as voted)'. A closing statement prepared by the Town Accountant and next year's budget, in one PDF, under one label. All twelve annual town reports carry `forward`, which would make the special revenue schedule and the combined balance sheet look like budget documents when each ties to its own printed totals every year. Nothing published rests on this being wrong, because those datasets are validated by their own control totals rather than by the basis label — but the column cannot be used to answer 'is this figure ledger-backed', which is what it looks like it answers. — closes: nothing external. This is ours to fix: a basis per table family in `annual_report_catalogue`, set where the reconciliation is already known, rather than one per document in `document-basis.csv`.

what: What any individual sport actually costs
why: Three documents state per-sport costs and they disagree — see “Which of the three published per-sport athletics cost figures is correct”, which supersedes this row's original claim that the district's own athletics workbook was the only place per-sport costs appear. The district has publicly declined to stand behind the figures: School Committee minutes of 24 June 2026 record that community members 'have asked straightforward questions regarding the actual cost of middle school athletics' and that 'the answers have been inconsistent'. The one independent record we hold does not reconcile to the workbook — in FY2024 the revolving fund paid out $317,004 and the general fund carried $285,281 against a stated workbook cost of $351,643, and nothing published explains the difference. And the fund's own disbursements cannot close it either: each carries a warrant number and nothing else, with no vendor, no description, and not one mention of any sport across three years of transactions. So participations, fees, and the fund's total in and out are established; what a sport costs is not. — closes: the accounts-payable detail behind the athletics warrants — vendor and description per payment — which the town's accounting system holds and does not publish.

what: Why a budget line came in under plan, as against by how much
why: A line under plan can be a post left vacant, a service cut, a grant that covered the cost instead, money transferred to another line, or a line over-budgeted from the start. All five produce the same smaller number in the spent column. The accounting system narrows it — it records mid-year transfers, so money moved can be distinguished from money not spent, and we hold that for FY2026 — but it cannot separate a vacancy from a cancelled service from a funding switch. Every published explanation of a Lunenburg school surplus is therefore a hypothesis about a measurement, and this project must not restate one as the measurement. — closes: payroll detail by position and date for the year in question, which separates a vacancy from every other cause, plus the grant award records for the same year.

what: Whether a school line that stops appearing in the district’s book stopped being funded
why: A line can leave the book because the money stopped, or because the book changed shape. Both look identical: an absence. Between FY2022 and FY2023 the restated series moves from one district budget book to another, the number of printed lines falls by about a third, and the reported total RISES — so the lines that stop appearing at that boundary cannot have taken their money with them. At least five of the disappearances are established renames, two lines differing only in spelling and carrying the identical value in every year they share (`Maint. of Buildings/Contrcted Services` and `Maint. of Buildings/Contracted Services`). Nothing published maps the older line list onto the newer one, so for any individual line, absence is a fact about the document and not about the service. — closes: the district’s own crosswalk from the FY2022 budget-book line list to the FY2023 presentation, or the MUNIS year-end expense report (glytdbud, period 13) for the school department for those years, which is keyed on accounts rather than on printed line names.

what: Which school lines stopped being funded in FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025
why: The restated figures for those years come from the FY27 budget projection workbooks, which print a shorter line list and almost no zeros. Not one line in them goes from funded in one year to a printed zero in the next — so the measurement this project can make for FY2015 through FY2022 has no evidence at all for the three most recent years. That is a property of which document restates which year, not a finding that nothing stopped. — closes: a district budget book for FY2026 or later printing the full line list with prior-year columns, in the same shape as `fy24-approved-budget`.

what: What Lunenburg pays in school choice sending tuition, and for how many children
why: The town pays tuition to every district a Lunenburg child chooses into, and that money is assessed rather than appropriated: it sits inside the single `State Assessments (Outside Operating FY27)` line of $1,069,349 in the FY2027 Town Meeting booklet, which is never broken out. The archive now holds DESE’s count of the children — 58 leaving under school choice in SY2026 — and still not one figure for what they cost. The statutory base rate is $5,000 a child under M.G.L. c.76 §12B and is higher for special education, and no document in this archive states either, so every scenario of students transferring out is priced on an assumption. — closes: DLS Cherry Sheet CS 1-EB (estimated charges) for Lunenburg, which prints the school choice sending assessment on its own line.

what: What Chapter 70 aid would actually do if enrollment fell
why: MUCH NARROWER THAN IT WAS. DESE’s Chapter 70 trends workbook breaks the aid calculation into its named components, and for Lunenburg they show that this year’s aid is last year’s aid plus named increments — an identity that holds to the dollar in every one of the last seven years. In FY2026 the whole of the increase is the minimum aid increment, $240,450, which is exactly $150.00 for each of the 1,603 foundation pupils, and the foundation aid increment is zero. Over thirty-four years foundation enrollment fell in 17 and aid fell in 3 — FY1997, FY2010 and FY2011. DESE’s component columns show a reduction applied in FY2010 and FY2011; they start at FY2007, so nothing in this archive says why aid fell in FY1997. So the marginal aid attached to one foundation pupil is currently about $150 and not the $14,440 foundation budget per pupil. What is NOT established: that the Legislature sets the same minimum aid rate next year — it has ranged from $30 to $150 a pupil in the years published — nor what happens if a large enough enrollment fall moves the district off the minimum aid track, which no document here models. — closes: DESE’s preliminary Chapter 70 aid calculation for Lunenburg for the year in question, which states the foundation aid, minimum aid and hold-harmless components before the year is set.

what: How much of a school budget stops being spent when a student leaves
why: A student leaving removes revenue at once and in full. It removes cost only where a staffing or programme decision is taken, and nothing published says at what enrollment a class section is removed, a bus route is dropped or a teacher is not replaced. So the avoidable share of a per-pupil figure is an assumption in every scenario on this site, and it is the input the answer is most sensitive to: at the FY2027 appropriation per pupil, the difference between assuming none of it is avoidable and assuming all of it is is larger than the entire revenue effect being modelled. — closes: the district’s own staffing and section plan by grade — the document behind the School Committee’s 16 April 2025 discussion of "each grade, their size, and potential seats" — which states the class sizes at which a section is added or removed.

what: What period the school athletic family cap covers
why: The $1,500 family cap was set by the School Committee on 26 February 2025 and the minutes state the amount and no period: "with a family cap of $1500". The cap it replaced did state one — the LHS Athletics FAQ prints "Total Cap per season=$475.00" — so the schedule has moved from a stated period to none. The district workbook obtained by records request carries the per-student rates on three worksheets named for the three seasons and carries no family cap in any cell, so the corroboration that dates the other rates does not reach this one. Read per season and read per year, $1,500 is a different bill for the same family. The arithmetic argues for the annual reading — with the published FY2027 ladder a family of five children playing one sport each in one season reaches $1,375, still under the cap — but that is an inference from the cap being unreachable, not a statement in any document. — closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, which is the document the Superintendent’s August 2026 email to families attached or described.

what: What the six fees the district’s payment portal sells actually cost
why: The district’s RevTrak portal offers an Afterschool Activity Fee, a Chromebook Repair Fee, Extended Day & ELC, Field Trips, an LHS Parking Permit and a Primary Preschool Program. The portal renders in JavaScript and serves no amounts to a plain fetch, and no fee schedule for any of them appears in a budget book, a warrant or a set of minutes in this archive. So the existence of each fee is established and the amount of every one of them is not, and any total of what a Lunenburg family pays the schools in a year is a floor with six named items sitting above it. — closes: the district’s published schedule of student fees for the current year, listing every fee the portal charges with its amount.

what: What a fourth child in one family pays for high school athletics
why: The FY2027 schedule names a first, second and third child — $400, $300 and $225 — and stops. The FY2024 and FY2025 schedules did the same, and there the cap resolved it: the three published rates sum to exactly the $475 the FAQ prints as the cap, so a fourth child added nothing. That identity does not hold in FY2027, where the three rates sum to $925 against a $1,500 cap, so the fourth child is neither priced nor obviously free. A family of four children — the case residents ask about most often — therefore cannot be costed from anything published. — closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, stating the rate for each additional child or the point at which the ladder stops.

what: What FY2027 athletic fees are for anyone other than a full-paying high school family
why: The only account this archive has of the 2026-27 athletic fees is a Superintendent’s email to families in August 2026 that we do not hold, reported as four figures: a first, second and third child and a family cap. FY2026 published more than that — a middle school rate, a reduced rate for high school and for middle school, and a sibling discount — and none of those has an FY2027 successor in any document here. So a middle school family, a family paying the reduced fee and a family whose fee is waived cannot be priced for the year now running. — closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, in full, including the reduced and waived rates and the middle school schedule.

what: How the $1,500 athletic family cap was arrived at, and over what period
why: The School Committee minutes of 26 February 2025 record the decision and not the derivation: "A slideshow presentation of athletic user fees is presented ... with a family cap of $1500. ... all approve via roll call vote". A slideshow WAS presented, so the arithmetic exists somewhere; this archive does not hold it, and the only athletics presentation material here is two Athletic Advisory Council agendas from the preceding weeks. Minutes summarise, so the absence of arithmetic in them is not evidence that there was none — what is established is that no document we hold derives the figure or states the period it covers. The figure itself is unreachable per season by family size alone: five children at one sport each come to between $1,220 and $1,375 depending on how the sibling discount is carried past the third child, both under $1,500. — closes: the athletic user fee presentation given to the School Committee on 26 February 2025, which is the slideshow the minutes name.

what: Which of the three published per-sport athletics cost figures is correct
why: NARROWED 5 October 2026: one of the three is now traced to its workbook. The Finance Committee's files hold `Athletics Costs (1).xlsx`, whose FY24 Programmatic Cost column (sheet ALL, rows 2-26) sums to 275,947.63 -- the published 'Athletic Program Costs by Sport' total -- once cell K26 is counted: Girls Ice Hockey, typed as the TEXT *1100, an estimate. The workbook's own printed total, 255,042.35, comes from =SUM(K3:K26), which leaves out both row 2 (Football, 19,805.28) and that text cell. So that figure was built from these rows, an estimate included; it does not say which of the three is correct. Three documents the district produced state three different costs for the same team in the same year, FY2024. Across all 25 teams they total $185,355.62 (the Athletic Program Funding Overview deck of 1 May 2024), $275,947.63 (“Athletic Program Costs by Sport”, published with the FY26 budget materials) and $349,145.39 (the Total Expenses column of the district’s own by-sport workbook, obtained by records request) — a spread of $163,789.77, 88.4%. Per team it is far wider: Boys' Lacrosse is stated at $612.79 and at $14,189.18, 2215.5% apart, and not one of the 25 teams carries the same figure in every column. The three may be answering different questions — a programmatic cost, an all-in cost and a season’s booked expenses would all differ legitimately — but no document we hold says which each column is, and nothing published reconciles them. So a resident choosing which sport to give up is choosing between figures that disagree by a multiple. — closes: a reconciliation from the district of its own three per-sport cost statements, sport by sport, naming what each column counts.

what: What folding one athletics team would actually stop the town spending
why: A per-sport figure is not a saving. The district’s own workbook divides district-wide costs into thirds and pushes them into season totals — the notes column headed “Costs for all 3 Seasons” reads, at AX6, “MIAA 1/3 4550. -1516.67”, and at AY10 “MIDWACH - 1/3 7000 - 2333.33” — so league membership, trainer supplies, CPR certification and the online forms subscription sit inside per-sport totals. Whether any of those actually falls when one team folds is untested: a league assessment, a trainer’s hours and an insurance premium may each scale with the number of teams or not at all. This app answers it structurally rather than empirically — the FY27 athletics lines are split into a coaching-and-equipment pool that follows the teams and an overhead that does not, and the published per-sport figures are used only as weights to spread the pool — which bounds the saving without establishing it. — closes: the district’s athletics budget for a year in which a team was actually dropped, line by line against the year before, or a quotation from the MIAA and MIDWACH showing how each assessment varies with the number of teams entered.

what: Whether a rise in the paraprofessional line is more posts or a grant unwinding
why: DESE now publishes the split at the level of its own FUNCTION CODES, SY2009-SY2025: Lunenburg's function 2330, Paraprofessionals, is $1,338,477 of general fund beside $478,097 of grants and revolving money in SY2025 (`dese_function_expenditure`). That BOUNDS the question and does not settle it. A function code aggregates many posts and many funding sources; it is DESE's measure of spending rather than the town's appropriation; and nothing in it says which post any dollar paid, or whether the same posts were general-funded the year before. The in-district special education escalator still rests on a line that cannot be distinguished from grant money unwinding. — closes: the district's grant award and payroll charge detail for the paraprofessional posts, by fund and fiscal year.

what: Which budget line each dollar of grant and revolving money paid for
why: The fund split now exists at DESE's function level and nowhere below it. Lunenburg SY2025 spent $3,044,898 of grants and revolving money against $26,986,344 of general fund across all functions. But the district's budget book prints one NET figure per printed line (rule 11), DESE prints one figure per function code, and no published document maps the second onto the first — so a line that rose because a grant ended still looks identical to a line that rose because the district grew. This is the budget-line half of `Which fund pays which post`, which is the same wall approached from the staffing side. — closes: DESE's End of Year Financial Report Schedule 1 as Lunenburg files it, which separates revenues and expenditures by source of funds; or the MUNIS year-to-date expense report run for the school grant and revolving funds rather than the general fund.

what: What the foundation budget pays per pupil for each kind of child
why: DESE builds the foundation budget from per-pupil rates that differ by grade and by category, and it publishes the CATEGORIES for Lunenburg — FY2026 foundation enrollment of 1,603, of whom 54 are English learners (3.4%), 452 are low income (28.8%, low-income group 5) and none is vocational, at a wage adjustment factor of 1.000 — without publishing the rate attached to any of them in the same file. So which children leave a district changes the foundation effect and not only how many, and this archive can state that it matters and cannot size it. — closes: DESE’s FY26 foundation budget rate schedule, the table of per-pupil rates by grade and category and the low-income increment by decile group.

what: What a DESE special education FTE and a district special education budget line have in common
why: DESE's `dese_sped_indicator` publishes special education paraprofessionals per 100 students with disabilities; times the published count that implies about 18 FTE for SY2026 against a district paraprofessional line that has roughly doubled since SY2019, which works out at some $69,000 per FTE. **A paraprofessional does not cost $69,000, so the two are not measurements of the same population.** The EPIMS Data Handbook gives half the reason: it defines FTE as *“the percent of workday staff are involved in an assignment”* — per ASSIGNMENT, not per person — while a budget line pays whole salaries. The other half is vocabulary: the district calls a line *Special Ed Paraprofessionals* and DESE has its own definition of a paraprofessional on the return, and neither is wrong. WHAT IS ESTABLISHED is that the two figures cannot both describe the same set of people. WHAT IS NOT is which is narrower, or by how much, or whether the line carries anything besides paraprofessionals. — closes: the district’s own crosswalk between its budget line names and what it reports to the state on EPIMS, which may exist nowhere in writing and would then be a records request rather than a download.

what: Why DESE special education teacher FTE falls from 18.5 to 2.0 while total teacher FTE holds flat
why: `dese_teacher_program_area` shows Lunenburg’s special education teacher FTE at 18.5 in SY2008 and 2.0 in SY2026 — a 90% collapse — while general education FTE holds between 100 and 113 and the district total is flat. A district that had lost nine tenths of its special education teachers would show it everywhere else in these files and does not. Teachers being RECODED from special education to general education produces exactly this signature. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED is that any recoding happened: a change in how FTE is apportioned when one person works across categories, a change in DESE’s program-area definitions, and a real staffing change all fit the same series. Rule 6, and nothing in the archive tests it. — closes: EPIMS work assignment records for Lunenburg aggregated by job classification and program area by year, which would show whether the same people were reported under a different code.

what: How many children Lunenburg has with disabilities, given that DESE publishes three different counts
why: NARROWED, 8 September 2026, and the narrowing is itself the finding. The denominator behind the staffing ratios in `yamx-769q` is NOT unexplained: it equals the published IN-DISTRICT count exactly, in all six years the file covers, and the difference between it and the count printed beside it is the published out-of-district count to the child. Computed on every build by scripts/build_special_education.py, which fails rather than publishing the page if it stops reconciling. WHAT SURVIVES is a THIRD count: `dese_sped_movement` reports 10 to 26 fewer children on an IEP than `dese_sped_program` in every overlapping year, on a different enrollment figure, and nothing published states the census date or the inclusion rule behind either. — closes: DESE’s SIMS submission detail for Lunenburg stating the census date and the inclusion rule behind each published count.

what: Which Lunenburg budget lines the circuit breaker reimbursement offsets
why: `dese_circuit_breaker` gives the reimbursement the district receives for high-cost special education placements, split into instruction and tuition against transportation, FY2006 to FY2026. It is real money and it is not in the general fund appropriation the town votes. Rule 11: a tuition line that fell because circuit breaker rose is not a line that got cheaper, and the budget document cannot tell the two apart. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED is which lines it lands against, or whether the district budgets net of it — the workbook nets other lines down against expected receipts and says so in its own comments column, so this is not a hypothetical. — closes: the district’s circuit breaker revolving fund cashbook for the year, which shows what the receipt was spent on.

what: What was said at a meeting whose minutes the town published only as a photograph
why: 3,116 of the 12,015 agendas and sets of minutes this project holds (26%) contain no text a search can match. 3,096 are image scans, 3 draw their text as vector outlines, 14 are blank, 2 have a text layer our extractor could not read and 1 will not parse; a further 50 are listed by the town and not held here. WHAT THIS IS NOT: it is not evidence that anything was left unsaid. The words are on the page and the page is a picture of a page, so an unreadable document and a subject nobody raised produce the identical empty result. Rule 15a instructs everyone working here to search the meeting archive before concluding a thing was never discussed, and until this was measured that search silently skipped a quarter of the record while printing a coverage line saying otherwise. IT IS NOT EVEN: the coverage is not evenly spread, so an archive-wide figure understates the boards that carry it — Board of Assessors 255 of 488 (52%); Select Board 629 of 1,347 (47%); Lunenburg Housing Authority 110 of 255 (43%). Measured per board and year in sources/data/minutes-searchable.csv, which scripts/build_minutes_searchable.py regenerates and check_generated.py refuses to let go stale. — closes: OCR of the image-only documents, already on the roadmap in notes/QUEUE.md, which recovers the scans and the vector-outline pages but produces OUR rendering rather than the town's own words (rule 13) and so must never be quoted as the document's text; and, for the documents the town lists that we do not hold, a records request to the Town Clerk for the minutes of the named meetings in a text-bearing format.

what: When was a meeting recording made, where the title does not say?
why: The PEG channel’s video titles are the only chronology there is: a flat channel extraction returns no upload dates, and 652 of the 4,671 titles state no date at all (as indexed 8 September 2026). For those the recording can be placed only by its position in the channel listing, which is not a date. — closes: the channel’s own per-video publication date, which the YouTube Data API returns as `snippet.publishedAt`. Even that is an UPLOAD date and not the meeting date.

what: Which body met, for a recording whose title names none?
why: 14 of 4,671 videos are `undetermined` — `Informational Symposium`, `Lunenburg Town Charrette . FULL`, `Master Plan Public Forum`, `School Funding Forum`, `911 YouTube`. The title is all we fetch; the channel also carries a description field on each video and several of these titles say "See Description". — closes: the per-video description text from the channel, which the index does not currently store.

what: Was a meeting recorded at all, when no video was posted?
why: The video index establishes THAT a recording was posted, which is a fact the written record does not always carry — the town posts minutes for a fraction of the meetings it holds. It cannot establish the reverse: a meeting recorded and not posted, or held and not recorded, looks identical from here. — closes: the PEG station’s own cablecast log, which lists what was recorded rather than what was uploaded.

what: How many meetings the town held, and how many of them left no record at all
why: This project can count meetings it has EVIDENCE of — 7,014 occasions where an agenda, a set of minutes or a recording says a board met on a day. It cannot count meetings. The town publishes documents rather than a schedule of what took place, so a meeting with no agenda, no minutes and no recording is indistinguishable from a meeting that never happened, and neither appears in sources/data/meeting-register.csv. That the gap is real rather than theoretical is shown by the meetings that survive on ONE thread: 231 occasions have a recording and no paperwork whatever, 162 of them School Committee, and 2,395 have an agenda announcing the meeting and no minutes saying what happened. Each of those would have been invisible if the other source had also been missing. WHAT THIS IS NOT: it is not a finding that the town met in secret. Open Meeting Law notice and the filing of minutes are separate obligations, and nothing here establishes which unrecorded meetings were noticed. — closes: the Town Clerk’s own record of meetings posted under the Open Meeting Law, which is a list of meetings NOTICED rather than a list of documents published, and is the only source that would give this register a denominator it did not derive from its own contents.

what: Whether a general fund rise beside a grant fall is the same cost, or a different cost in the same function
why: DESE's End of Year Financial Report splits every function code into general fund and grants/revolving, so a function where grants fell and the general fund rose in the same year can be MEASURED — 8 of them in Lunenburg in SY2025, grants -$1,127,647 against general fund +$1,136,013 (`dese_function_expenditure`). Sorting those functions into “swapped” and “reduced” is OUR label on the signs of two numbers, and the state publishes no such classification. A function code is a bucket: `Teachers, Classroom` covers every classroom teacher in four schools, and both funds can move inside it for reasons that have nothing to do with each other. So the split establishes that the funding mix moved and cannot establish that the town picked up the thing the grant was paying for. — closes: the district's grant award letters and end-of-grant expenditure reports, naming the posts and object codes each grant paid, set against the general fund payroll and object detail for the same function in the following year.

what: How much of the SY2025 grant fall was ESSER, as against every other grant and revolving fund
why: The meeting record names ESSER as the cause repeatedly and with figures — the district told the School Committee on 15 November 2023 “We have a loss of $650,000 in ESSER funds, this is much more significant than we expected”, and on 17 January 2024 put the loss at $600,000 beside a $500,000 health insurance rise. DESE reports one combined `grants_revolving` column, which holds ESSER, Title I and the other federal and state grants together with circuit breaker, school choice, athletics, food service and every other revolving fund. The SY2025 fall of $2,023,188 across matched functions therefore cannot be attributed to any one of them. The district's own stated ESSER figures and this fall are different quantities measured at different stages — a forward budget gap against a closed-year fund total — and this project does not difference one against the other. — closes: the district's end-of-year grant expenditure detail by grant code for FY2024 and FY2025, or Schedule 19 of its End of Year Financial Report as filed, which lists each grant separately.

what: Why Chapter 70 aid moved by more than the components DESE publishes, in FY2010, FY2011, FY2012 and FY2019
why: DESE’s Chapter 70 trends workbook prints the aid build-up as named increments — foundation aid, down payment aid, growth aid, target aid phase-in, minimum aid — and in fifteen of the nineteen differenced years they sum to the change in aid to the dollar. In four they do not. FY2010 and FY2011 carry a separate `c70aidreduct` column of −$92,416 and −$279,101, and only the first of the two accounts for its year; FY2012 moved +$24,149 with every increment printed as zero; FY2019 moved $13,365 more than its single increment. The workbook prints no residual line, so the difference has no name in the source. It matters because this page reads the components to say what the formula did, and in those four years the components do not add up to what it did. — closes: DESE’s Chapter 70 aid calculation worksheet for FY2010, FY2011, FY2012 and FY2019, which states every adjustment applied to a district between the prior year’s aid and the current year’s.

what: Which cell of DESE’s contribution sheet is mislabelled in FY2020
why: In eighteen of the nineteen differenced years the town’s preliminary contribution equals the previous year’s required contribution multiplied by that year’s municipal revenue growth factor, exactly as DESE’s own User Guide defines it, and the required contribution is that figure adjusted toward target. In FY2020 the two are the other way round: `dataContribution!O2593` prints $10,427,328, which is FY2019’s required contribution un-grown, and `dataContribution!U2593` prints $10,889,259, which is that figure grown by the 4.43% factor. One of the two cells is carrying the other’s quantity and nothing in the workbook says which. The extract records what the sheet holds rather than repairing it. — closes: DESE’s FY2020 required local contribution worksheet for Lunenburg, which prints the preliminary contribution and the required contribution as separate stated steps.

what: Which of DESE’s special education staff figures can be read at all
why: Every row of the SPECIAL EDUCATION STAFF table in `yamx-769q` prints an FTE, a count of students and a rate per 100 of them, so the rate has to reproduce from the other two. Recomputed for Lunenburg on every build: paraprofessionals reproduce in 8 of 8 years, teachers in 1 of 8, service FTE in 0 of 7, support FTE in 0 of 6. So three of the four rows do not describe what their own column headings say, and /how-many-students-are-on-an-iep publishes the paraprofessional row and refuses to publish the others as figures. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED is which of the three columns is the one that is wrong. — closes: DESE’s data dictionary for dataset yamx-769q, or the EPIMS aggregation behind it, stating what each column is.

what: How many of the children who leave Lunenburg under school choice have an IEP
why: DESE publishes where every town’s resident children are enrolled, by district and by programme — 58 leaving under school choice in SY2026, 22 at charter schools, 97 at Montachusett Regional as members — and publishes NO disability status with it. So a special education student who transfers out and a student with no plan who transfers out are one row. This is why /where-students-go-instead is a separate report from the other three special education pages rather than a section inside one: merged, “58 children left” becomes “58 special education children left” in a single retelling. — closes: DESE’s SIMS detail crossing enrollment reason with IEP status, which is not published at town level at all.

what: Over what period does DESE’s placement trajectory measure movement
why: Dataset 92x3-2qj9 follows a cohort from the setting its placement started in to where the same children are now, and it is the only published route into out-of-district placement. The workbook is a single Data sheet with no notes, and nothing in it or on the portal page states the interval between the start and the destination. Every rate drawn from it — including the finding that Lunenburg children who started in a substantially separate classroom are out of district about fifteen times as often as those who started in an inclusive setting — is a rate over an unstated span, so none of them can be annualised or compared with a rate measured over a known one. — closes: DESE’s methodology note for dataset 92x3-2qj9, stating the cohort rule and the interval.

what: How many out-of-district placements are children who arrived already placed
why: The trajectory file measures the route through the district’s own settings, and the district told the School Committee on 4 February 2026 that “we have also had students move into the district that require out of district placements”. Such a child enters the town’s placement count without ever appearing in a cohort followed from an in-district setting, so the count and the route measure overlapping but different populations. The quote is evidence that it happens; nothing establishes how often, and the two published counts of placed children — the town’s on 1 March and DESE’s — agree in only 2 of the 5 years they overlap. — closes: the district’s own record of placements by origin, showing how many were referred from an in-district setting and how many arrived already placed.

what: Which grades Lunenburg children leave the district in
why: DESE publishes where a town’s resident children go to school and by which route — school choice, charter, regional vocational — by receiving district and by year, FY2014 to FY2026. It does not publish that by GRADE. dese_town_enrollment carries no grade column, and the grade counts that do exist (dese_enrollment) are headcounts INSIDE a district rather than an outflow from a town, so they cannot be differenced to recover it. WHAT THIS BLOCKS: the question everyone actually asks, which is whether families leave at a transition year — entering grade 9, or entering grade 7 — or steadily throughout. Those imply completely different things about what the district could change, and the published data cannot tell them apart. IT IS NOT: an absence of evidence that transitions matter. It is an absence of evidence either way, and the plausible story (that choice-outs cluster at grade 9 when families pick a high school) is a hypothesis nothing here tests. — closes: DESE SIMS Report 7 or the district’s own October 1 enrollment submission broken out by grade and residence, which the district files annually and does not publish; or the receiving districts’ school choice enrollment by sending town and grade.

what: Why these six districts and not six others
why: Every comparison on this page runs against a set of six districts chosen by this project — Ashburnham-Westminster, Ayer Shirley, Groton-Dunstable, Harvard, North Middlesex and Lunenburg. DESE’s RADAR workbook covers all 421 Massachusetts districts and this archive extracts six because the full file takes the published database past Cloudflare’s per-asset limit. No document here records the criterion by which those six were picked, and a peer set is an argument: whoever chooses it has already made a claim about what Lunenburg is comparable to. That is why every headline figure on /what-other-districts-spend is stated against DESE’s statewide distribution of 318 districts rather than against the six. — closes: DESE’s own DART comparison group for Lunenburg, which names the districts the Department considers similar and states the criteria it used.

what: What DESE’s per-pupil figure buys
why: DESE publishes dollars over a pupil count, by function, for every district. It does not publish what those dollars bought: a Teachers line is not a class size, an Instructional Materials line is not a textbook count, and a Paraprofessional FTE is not a person or a caseload. So Lunenburg spending $226 a pupil on instructional materials, equipment and technology against a statewide median of $626 is a measured difference in money and not a measured difference in what children have. Rule 7’s standing form: dollars are not services. — closes: the district’s own inventory and purchasing records for the materials and technology line, which would say what was bought and when.

what: Whether Lunenburg’s MCAS results are high or low for Massachusetts
why: Residents have argued the comparison in both directions at School Committee — that the town is “in the top 20% for school performance while being in the bottom 10% for spending”, and that “neighboring districts… have faced similar challenges while achieving stronger outcomes”. The spending half of that can be checked here, because DESE publishes the statewide distribution of per-pupil spending with quartiles and a rank. The results half cannot: this archive holds MCAS for six districts and no statewide distribution of it at all, so no percentile, rank or state median can be computed for any of the four measures. — closes: DESE’s district-level MCAS achievement file for all districts, published per year at profiles.doe.mass.edu, extracted the way the finance distribution already is.

what: Whether spending less per pupil is a choice or a constraint
why: Lunenburg’s total per-pupil spending has been below the statewide first quartile in every one of the seventeen years DESE publishes, and its net school spending is a smaller multiple of the required minimum than the median district’s. Nothing in any of these documents distinguishes a town that decided to spend less from a town that could not raise more: the levy limit, two failed overrides, the district’s proposed budget and Town Meeting’s vote all resolve into the same single number, and the number is the outcome of all of them at once. This matters because the two readings imply opposite remedies. — closes: nothing published settles it; the nearest evidence is the district’s own level-service request against the appropriation voted, year by year, which the archive holds for FY2024 onward only.

what: Whether Lunenburg spends the foundation budget the way the state assumes it will, category by category
why: Chapter 70 builds its foundation budget from about eleven CATEGORIES — classroom teachers, administration, instructional leadership, materials, and so on — each with a per-pupil rate the state sets. That is the state saying what an adequate education costs and how it decomposes. Comparing it line for line against what the district actually spends on the same categories would show exactly where Lunenburg is above and below the state’s own model, and it is the single most useful unanswered question about the expense side. WE HOLD THE TOTAL AND NOT THE PARTS. dese-ch70-foundation-nss.xlsx carries required net school spending, actual net school spending and the foundation budget as single figures per district per year, and dese-ch70-key-factors.xlsx carries the aid calculation; neither breaks the foundation budget into its categories. So the comparison cannot be made from this archive at all, in any year. WHAT MUST NOT BE DONE INSTEAD: dividing the foundation total by DESE’s statewide category shares to estimate Lunenburg’s. That produces a number for every category and establishes nothing, because the shares are what the comparison is meant to test. — closes: DESE’s foundation budget detail workbook, which prints the per-pupil rates and the resulting category amounts for every district, published annually beside the Chapter 70 aid figures this project already holds.

what: How the Monty Tech assessment splits between operating, transportation and capital
why: A regional assessment is four parts, and the district names them: required minimum contribution set by the state, transportation and other operating above minimum net school spending, capital outlay, and bonds. The split is published for FY2024, FY2026 and FY2027 in the district’s own budget books, and for FY2023 it was itemised in prose at a Finance Committee meeting. Every other year holds only the total. That includes FY2025, and it includes all eleven annual-report years FY2011 to FY2022 — so for the whole of the series this project charts, the roughly 4-10% of the assessment sitting above the state minimum cannot be attributed to transportation, to capital or to debt. It matters because those three behave nothing alike: one tracks a busing contract, one is voted year by year, and one is fixed until it ends. — closes: the district’s annual assessment certification to each member town, which states the four components separately; the Town Accountant receives one every year and the district retains all of them.

what: How the Montachusett regional agreement apportions costs among its member towns
why: The apportionment method is now on the record twice: the district printed it in Lunenburg’s FY2017 annual town report — four parts, with transportation and other operating divided by each town’s 1 October enrollment share and capital divided by each town’s school-attending children in grades 1 to 12 — and DESE’s own apportionment sheet, reprinted in the FY2027 budget presentation, shows the required-contribution part split between a town’s two districts by foundation-budget share. WHAT IS STILL MISSING IS THE INSTRUMENT. A budget book states current practice; the regional agreement is what binds it, and it is the document that would say whether the ratios can be changed, how bonds are apportioned and over what term, what a member town’s withdrawal would require, and what amendments have been made. Asked at the Finance Committee on 5 February 2026 whether the agreement was indefinite or could be renegotiated, the Superintendent-Director said he believed it was ongoing and that amendments were very rare. A recollection at a meeting is not the instrument. — closes: the Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School District regional agreement and its amendments, filed with the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education and held by the district and by each member town’s clerk.

what: Why the district and the town state different FY2027 Monty Tech assessments
why: Monty Tech’s FY2027 budget presentation puts Lunenburg’s total assessment at $1,452,379, built from a required minimum contribution of $1,378,183 and a transportation and operating assessment of $74,196 with no capital and no bonds. The Town’s own FY2027 operating budget book carries the same line at $1,452,426, in all three of its scenarios. The difference is $47 and neither document acknowledges the other. It is small enough to be a rounding or a late revision and it is not nothing: the two figures are the district’s bill and the town’s appropriation for the same year, and every other year in this archive where both exist ties to the dollar or to eighteen cents. — closes: the district’s FY2027 assessment certification to the Town of Lunenburg, and the Monty Tech line as finally voted at Annual Town Meeting.

what: When the town actually posted an agenda or a set of minutes, as against when we first saw it
why: The AgendaCenter lists a document's MEETING date and publishes no posting date anywhere -- not in the listing markup, not in the file's URL, not in the response headers. So scripts/watch_meetings.py can record only `first_seen`, the day this project's crawler first observed a document, and the gap between a meeting and its minutes appearing is bounded by how often we look rather than measured. Every such field in sources/data/meeting-watch-events.csv and in fy28/public/data/meeting-feed.json is named `days_after_meeting_upper_bound` for that reason. WHAT IT IS NOT: it is not a measurement of how long the town takes, and a document posted the day after a meeting and one posted three weeks later are indistinguishable if we looked once in between. It is also blind backwards: the 12,065 documents the watch adopted when it was seeded on 8 September 2026 carry no first_seen at all -- an empty cell rather than a guess -- so no lag figure exists for anything published before that date, and the series begins the day the watch did. The separate question of how many meetings the town HELD is registered above, “How many meetings the town held, and how many of them left no record at all”. -- closes: the CivicEngage AgendaCenter's own record of when each document was uploaded, which the platform stores and the public listing does not render; the Town Clerk or the site administrator can export it.

what: What Monty Tech spends, and on what
why: Lunenburg is assessed $1,334,521 for Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical in FY2026 and that figure is what the town is BILLED, not what educating 101 foundation pupils costs. PART OF THIS ROW HAS CLOSED. DESE’s RADAR district comparison publishes an all-funds per-pupil total for LEA 08320000 for FY2009 to FY2025 — seventeen consecutive years, every one of them summing to the workbook’s own printed in-district total — so the district’s per-pupil spending CAN now be tracked over time and set beside Lunenburg Public Schools’ own, measured the same way, which is what /what-other-districts-spend does. WHAT REMAINS OPEN is the composition and the attribution. RADAR gives ten per-pupil function columns and no dollars, no fund split and nothing specific to Lunenburg’s children; the archive holds two of the district’s own budget books — the FY2024 hearing book and the FY2027 presentation — so a FY24-to-FY27 view by DESE function code exists in dollars, with no year before FY2024 and nothing for the years between the two books. So what the district spends on a Lunenburg child, as against on any child, is still not established. — closes: Monty Tech’s annual budget book for each year, presented to its own School Committee and to the Lunenburg Finance Committee every March, and DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for LEA 08320000, which gives all-funds spending by function in dollars after the year closes.

what: How many Lunenburg applicants Monty Tech turns away
why: Lunenburg’s count at Monty Tech has risen in nine of the last twelve years, and a count is the outcome of two things at once: families applying, and Monty Tech admitting. The lottery exists precisely because more apply than there are places. Asked at the Finance Committee on 5 February 2026 how many Lunenburg students were turned away, the district’s business manager said she was unsure of the exact number. The Class of 2030 lottery result in this archive gives one cohort’s admissions — 24 Lunenburg students of 365 places — and its per-applicant pages are OCR of an image PDF and cannot be counted from. So a rising count cannot be read as rising demand, and the two have opposite implications for what the town should expect next. — closes: Monty Tech’s admissions summary by sending town and year — applications received, offers made, waitlisted — which the district produces for its own School Committee.

what: Why DESE’s foundation enrollment for Lunenburg at Monty Tech differs from its own October headcount
why: Two DESE counts of the same thing disagree in every year. The Chapter 70 foundation enrollment used to compute the assessment — derived on /monty-tech by subtracting the Lunenburg district’s from the town’s — runs between eight below and fifteen above the October headcount of Lunenburg residents attending Montachusett Regional in DESE’s own residents-by-district file, and the gap has no consistent sign or size. One documented mechanism puts children into the assessment who are not at Monty Tech: the district’s business director told the Finance Committee in March 2022 that four Lunenburg students attending trade programmes at Leominster and Nashoba “become part of the Monty Tech assessment”. That accounts for a difference in one direction and not for the years running the other way. Until it is reconciled, no per-student figure on this page can be quoted without saying which count is the denominator. — closes: DESE’s foundation enrollment detail for the Chapter 70 calculation, which states the collection date and the categories included, published beside the key factors workbook this project already holds.

what: What Lunenburg’s net school spending actually was in the two most recent years
why: DESE publishes net school spending against the Chapter 70 requirement for thirty-three fiscal years, and the last two of them are BUDGETED rather than actual — the column carries a stage flag saying so. So the most recent MEASURED position Lunenburg has against the state is FY2024, and every statement about where the town sits NOW rests on a budget somebody voted rather than on money anybody spent. The two may not be differenced and are never drawn as one line, which is why /what-the-state-requires-us-to-spend carries them as separate series. — closes: DESE’s Chapter 70 district profile workbook for the year in which FY2025 moves into the actual column, published annually at educationtocareer.data.mass.gov; the district’s own End of Year Financial Report to DESE for FY2025 is the filing that produces it.

what: How the district’s own accounts add up to the net school spending DESE reports
why: NARROWED 5 October 2026 for FY2024. the Finance Committee files received by records request on 4 October 2026 (`sources/budget-workbooks/finance-committee/`, see its PROVENANCE note) include the district's FY24 End of Year Financial Report workbook, whose own Schedule 19 states net school spending as 22,496,198 (`reports` sheet, row 28) -- a working copy, so DESE's filed figure governs. Net school spending excludes debt service, capital, transportation and food service — stated in the town’s own record, to the Finance Committee on 20 March 2024: “This is the minimum spending every school district must spend not including debt services, capital transportation, meals.” Because of those exclusions no figure in the town’s appropriation, the district’s budget book or the MUNIS ledger equals the net school spending DESE reports, and nothing in this archive maps the district’s line items onto DESE’s definition. So a reader cannot get from a budget line they can see to the one number the state enforces. — closes: the district’s End of Year Financial Report as filed with DESE, whose schedules derive net school spending from the district’s own accounts line by line; requestable from the Superintendent’s office or from DESE.

what: What the student activity fee is for 2026-27, and what period the $70 covers
