The two agree on all 17 other towns and on all 18 Required Minimum Contributions to the dollar. Only page 148's column foots to the District Total of 1,496 that BOTH pages print; page 144's 18 rows sum to 1,495, although its own per-row Change identities all close. Foundation enrolment is the input Chapter 70 runs on, so a member town's count is load-bearing for every town's assessment — and neither page says which of its own figures is the error. — closes: DESE's published FY18 Chapter 70 regional district enrolment file for LEA 832 Montachusett, at doe.mass.edu, which is the source both pages reproduce.

what: Which department carried forward the $362.00 the FY2017 appropriations schedule does not print?
why: The FY2017 GENERAL FUND APPROPRIATIONS schedule, pages 24-28 of the annual town report, states twice that a $362.00 carry-forward exists and never prints the line. Its APPROPRIATED FORWARD column sums to $37,626,083.44 against a printed GRAND TOTAL of $37,626,445.44, and its footer legend `fwd - forward from FY 2016 $637,981.43` exceeds the 26 fwd lines actually printed by the same $362.00 — while the srt and rft legend totals reproduce to the cent and the other three columns tie exactly. The subtotal for Police Fire Medical Expenses on page 25 is $5,362.00 over a single line item of $5,000.00, so the money belongs to that block; which prior-year appropriation it is a carry-forward OF is not stated anywhere in the document. The amount is trivial; the question is not, because the same schedule is the basis of every departmental growth rate this project measures and a carry-forward line changes which year a dollar belongs to. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2017 year-end MUNIS encumbrance and carry-forward detail, which lists each forwarded balance by account.

what: Which of the FY2020 receipts the Town collected are TAXES & EXCISES, which are FEES, and which are NON RECURRING REVENUE?
why: The Treasurer's FY2020 receipts page (annual town report PDF p24) prints 100 line items in three free-form label/amount columns with NO column header, and a SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS block of nine categories footing to a GRAND TOTAL of $43,089,202.54. Both halves of the page were read off its own embedded bitmap on 2 October 2026 and both close to the cent: the 100 detail lines add to the GRAND TOTAL, and so, separately, do the nine summary lines. Six of the nine categories are defined by a heading the page prints above their lines and each foots exactly -- licenses and permits $331,254.75 (19 lines), state revenue $9,790,141.52 (12), special assessments $68,681.50 (3), fines and forfeits $37,182.61 (4), investment income $102,340.41 (1) and transfers from other funds $2,291,492.46 (1). The other three print no heading that separates them, and their 60 lines foot as ONE block to $30,468,109.29, the sum of the three printed category totals. A residual does fit -- moving SUPPL TAX-NEW CONSTRUCTION $10,057.81 out of taxes and $100,180.88 of RESCUE WAGON out of non-recurring would close all three -- but that is arithmetic choosing a grouping rather than the document stating one, and other partitions fit the same three printed totals equally well. So we can say what the town took in, and not how it classified 60 of the lines. This is the SAME gap already registered for FY2021 and it is a property of the form, not of one year. -- closes: the Treasurer's own receipts workbook for FY2020, the file the page is printed from, which carries the category each line is coded to. Not published; a records request to the Town Treasurer would obtain it.

what: Does the FY2018 debt repayment schedule's printed grand total account for every issue's INTEREST?
why: IN FY2019 IT DOES NOT, BY THE EXACT INTEREST OF ONE ISSUE. Pages 48-51 of the FY2018 annual town report print sixteen debt issues against FY2019-FY2047 and, separately, GRAND TOTAL rows per year. Read in full, the issues reconcile to those grand totals within $2 in all 29 years -- the schedule shows whole dollars over amounts carrying cents -- except FY2019, where the issues' interest exceeds the printed GRAND TOTAL INTEREST by 272 and TOTAL DEBT by the same 272 while principal ties EXACTLY. 272 is precisely the FY2019 interest of MASS WATER POOL 4*, whose own row closes to the dollar (10,409 + 272 = 10,681) and whose 10,409 of principal IS inside the grand total. So one of the two printed figures is wrong and the document does not say which; the archive publishes both and asserts neither. This is the same defect the FY2015 row in this register names for PRINCIPAL, in a different year and a different column, and the two may be worth merging. - closes: the Treasurer's own debt service schedule for FY2019, or the Massachusetts Clean Water Trust (formerly MWPAT) amortization schedule for Pool 4, either of which states that loan's FY2019 interest and admin fee independently of the town's own summary.

what: Which figure did the 2018 Annual Town Meeting actually vote where the printed FY 2019 Omnibus Budget does not add up?
why: The budget as printed on pages 155-158 of the FY2018 annual town report carries TWO arithmetic misprints and the document contradicts itself about both. `Total General Government $1,401,119.25` is 709.00 MORE than the 22 lines beneath it, and the printed `Total Omnibus $36,804,408.83` agrees with the subtotal rather than with the lines. `Total Assistance $243,493.56` is 2,000.00 LESS than the two subtotals above it, and there the Total Omnibus agrees with the subtotals rather than with the line. Ten of the twelve section totals foot their own line items to the cent, every subtotal foots exactly, and the pages carry a digital text layer, so this is the town's arithmetic and not our reading. What a resident cannot tell from the published report is which number was put to the meeting: the appropriation is voted as one sum, and a 709.00 or 2,000.00 difference changes what the departments beneath it were authorised to spend. - closes: the Town Clerk's certified record of the vote on Article 7 of the 5 May 2018 Annual Town Meeting, which states the sum voted and the schedule attached to it.

what: Which fiscal year did Town Meeting vote the left-hand half of the FY 2016 Omnibus Budget for?
why: The omnibus schedule on pages 140-141 of the FY2015 annual town report is titled `FY 2016 Omnibus Budget` and is set as two panels per page. Its right panel is headed `VOTED FY 2016` and its left panel `VOTED FY 2015`. Everything else on the page says it is one column: the line numbers run 1 to 82 continuously across both panels and both pages, the 91 line items sum exactly to the single TOTAL OMNIBUS of $32,025,895.00, and so do the twelve printed section totals. But the report itself never states which heading is wrong, and the arithmetic cannot tell a misprinted heading from a correct one. Until it is settled, no figure from the left panel may be cited as an FY2015 appropriation or as an FY2016 one without saying which. - closes: the Town Clerk's record of the vote at the 2015 Annual Town Meeting, with the warrant article and the amount as moved, which the town holds and does not publish.

what: What was the Town owed in motor vehicle excise, user charges and betterments at 30 June 2016?
why: THE FY2016 RECEIVABLES SUMMARY IS PRINTED CLIPPED, AND THE CLOSING COLUMNS ARE THE ONES CUT OFF. Page 47 of the FY2016 annual town report prints the property-tax half of the schedule with EIGHT columns -- FORWARD, COMMITTMENTS, ADJUSTMENTS, REFUNDS, PAYMENTS, ABATEMENTS, TRANSFER, BALANCES -- and every row closes on the identity those columns state. Page 48 (motor vehicle excise, twenty levy years) stops after PAYMENTS. Page 49 (deferred taxes, water and sewer user charges, utility liens, sewer/water/street/septic betterments, apportioned assessments) stops after REFUNDS, and its own title is cut mid-word -- `FY2016 COLLECTION OF TAXE`. Page 50 is blank but for its folio, so nothing continues. Both pages were rendered and looked at on 2 October 2026: the ruled table simply ends at the right-hand edge of the page. SO THERE IS NO PUBLISHED BALANCE for any of those accounts and no arithmetic on either page can be closed. The combined balance sheet on page 20 does not substitute: it prints one undivided `EXCISES $243,852.65` against page 48's five columns netting $303,306.05, which are not the same quantity. This is NOT the same gap as the FY2013/FY2017/FY2020 receivables refusals, which are about an extractor failing on pages that ARE fully printed -- here the document does not carry the figures. — closes: the Collector's and Treasurer's own FY2016 receivables control report, or an un-clipped printing of the same worksheet, which the Town Accountant's system can reproduce.

what: What else did the Town receive in FY2016 after CH 70 SCHOOL AID, and what did its receipts add up to?
why: THE FY2016 RECEIPTS PAGE IS CUT OFF MID-LIST AND PRINTS NO TOTAL. `FY 2016 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2016`, PDF page 23 of the annual town report, is a two-column list of about 54 figures. The left column ends at `RELEASE FEES` in the middle of the FEES block; the right column ends at `CH 70 SCHOOL AID` in the middle of the STATE REVENUE block. Both stop at the same height on the page, which is what a print that ran out of room looks like. There is no SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS block and no GRAND TOTAL anywhere on it. The comparison is the Town's own later practice: the FY2020 and FY2021 receipts pages print about 100 detail lines AND a nine-category summary footing to a printed grand total, which is what let both of those years be read and checked. FY2016 prints neither, so the page cannot be footed, the receipts cannot be classified into the Town's own categories, and what the Town took in during FY2016 is not stated in this report. — closes: the Treasurer's FY2016 cash receipts report as the accounting system produces it, the same report whose later editions the FY2020 and FY2021 annual reports print in full.

what: Which capital project is the unnamed $25,000.00 on the FY2016 capital projects schedule?
why: THE PAGE PRINTS A RULED ROW WITH A FIGURE AND NO NAME. On `CAPITAL PROJECT FUNDS FY 2016`, PDF page 36 of the FY2016 annual town report, the row between the column header and `08/02 ATM Development of Cemeteries` carries $25,000.00 in APPROPRIATED FORWARD and nothing else -- no purpose, no article reference, no `fwd` flag, no expended figure, no balance. IT IS NOT A READING ERROR AND IT IS NOT IGNORABLE. All three columns of the page tie to the printed Grand Total to the cent only when that $25,000.00 is counted, so the figure is part of the schedule. And the Cemeteries row immediately below it does not close as printed -- $1,019.01 less $35,229.38 is ($34,210.37) against a printed balance of ($9,210.37), short by exactly $25,000.00. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: that the $25,000.00 belongs to the Cemeteries project. A label that failed to print, a second article against the same project, and a separate project whose text was lost all fit the same evidence, and nothing in the report tests between them. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2016 capital project fund detail by article, which names the article every capital appropriation sits under.

what: What were Lunenburg’s fiscal 2011 class valuations, where the town’s own two printings disagree by $7,295,100?
why: The FY2011 annual town report prints the same quantity twice on one page (PDF p12, printed folio 9) and the two do not reconcile. `Fiscal 2011 Assessments and Revenues by Major Property Class` puts Commercial at 64,514,700 and foots its tax levy to the printed 18,006,811.48 to the cent; the `Fiscal Year 2011 Abstract of Assessments` below it puts `300 - 393 Commercial` at 56,208,300 and `600 - 821 Chapter 61, 61A, 61B` at 1,011,300, so its twelve classes sum to 1,106,987,789 against its own printed TOTALS of 1,114,282,889. The residual is 7,295,100 and it sits entirely in the commercial class: the abstract’s eight residential lines sum to 1,000,004,500, which is the first table’s Residential valuation to the dollar, and its account count ties exactly at 5,185, so no row is missing from the reading. Both cells were re-read off the page’s own 400 dpi bitmap at 6x. Which printing is wrong is not established, and the report itself settles nothing — the first table’s own TOTALS cell is misprinted `1,114,2828,889`, ten digits. — closes: the Assessors’ certified fiscal 2011 Tax Recapitulation (DOR Form LA-4/LA-5) for Lunenburg, which states valuation by class as the Department of Revenue certified it and is the only document that outranks both printings.

what: Which of the FY2011 receipts the Town collected are TAXES & EXCISES, which are FEES, and which are NON RECURRING REVENUE?
why: Page 58 of the FY2011 annual town report prints 90 receipt lines under ten block headings and then a nine-category `SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS` footed to a GRAND TOTAL of $27,388,537.87. The summary ties to the cent, and every detail figure on the page is now transcribed, but the page never says which detail line belongs to which category and the headings are not the categories — ten blocks against nine categories, one block unheaded, and `FEES` naming both a block and a category without the two agreeing. Five categories can be reproduced exactly (LICENSES AND PERMITS, STATE REVENUE, SPECIAL ASSESSMENTS, INVESTMENT INCOME, TRANSFER FROM OTHER FUNDS); four cannot. TAXES & EXCISES comes out $23,947.19 OVER its printed total, FINES & FORFEITS $2,025.00 SHORT, and FEES ($502,520.65) and NON RECURRING REVENUE ($71,325.29) cannot be reconstructed by any grouping the page states. So the town’s own revenue mix for FY2011 — how much is tax, how much is fee, how much is one-off — cannot be read off the document that reports it. This is the same limit already registered for FY2016, FY2020 and FY2021 and it recurs because the format does. — closes: the Treasurer’s or Accountant’s FY2011 receipts detail as the accounting system prints it, with each receipt account carrying its revenue classification (a MUNIS revenue report by account), which is the only document that states the mapping rather than assuming it.

what: What are the $25,276.56 of fines and $3,110.00 of fees that FY2012 receipts counts but does not name?
why: The FY2012 annual town report, PDF p58 (`FY 2012 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2012`), prints 91 detail lines and a nine-category SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS. The nine categories foot to the printed GRAND TOTAL of $28,471,842.32 exactly; the 91 lines sum to $28,443,455.76, short by $28,386.56. Seven of the nine categories are reproduced to the cent by a partition of those lines, which puts the whole shortfall in two: FINES & FORFEITS, where the page prints only PARKING FINES $2,120.25 and DOG FINES $2,550.00 against a category total of $29,946.81, and FEES, short by $3,110.00. The page was swept end to end and prints no further row, so this is the document omitting detail rather than our reading missing it. Court fines are the obvious candidate for the larger figure and nothing in the report says so. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2012 general ledger revenue detail (MUNIS), which lists every receipt account by code rather than by the summary categories this page prints.

what: Which figure is wrong in the FY2013 Omnibus Budget: the eleven section totals, or the $600 larger Total Omnibus?
why: The budget Town Meeting voted under Article 8 is printed in the FY2012 annual town report, PDF pp.81-82. Every one of its eleven sections foots to its own printed subtotal exactly, and those eleven subtotals sum to $27,488,841.00 against a printed `Total Omnibus` of $27,489,441.00 — six hundred dollars more. Both figures were re-read upright at full scale off the page's own 518 dpi bitmap, so this is the document disagreeing with itself and not a misreading. The $600 could be a line the page does not print, a section total understated, or the grand total overstated, and nothing on those two pages distinguishes them. — closes: the Town Clerk's certified copy of the Article 8 motion and the FY2013 budget handouts it refers to (`Refer to Handouts on pages 27 – 30`), which the annual report does not reproduce.

what: What the $600.00 is between the FY2013 receipts page's own detail and its own GRAND TOTAL
why: PDF page 63 of the FY2013 annual town report prints `FY 2013 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2013`: 91 detail lines in three label/amount column-pairs, and beside them a nine-line SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS footing to a printed GRAND TOTAL of $29,744,547.31. The nine summary categories sum to that GRAND TOTAL EXACTLY. The 91 detail lines sum to $29,743,947.31 -- $600.00 less. The reading is not the problem: the page has no text layer and was read off its own 400 dpi bitmap twice, and three of its printed detail blocks foot to their matching summary line to the cent (LICENSES/PERMITS to 174,193.45, STATE REVENUE to 7,010,803.56, FINES & FORFEITS to 27,405.00), which bounds the difference away from 29 of the 91 lines and leaves it inside the fees and departmental revenue lines. The page never states that the detail is exhaustive of the summary, so this is NOT recorded as the town's arithmetic failing -- it may be one receipt listed only in the summary, a line printed $600 low, or two different universes. Nothing on the page distinguishes them. sources/data/page-reads/fy2013-p63-*.csv. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2013 year-end revenue report out of the accounting system (the MUNIS revenue ledger for fiscal 2013, which this project already holds for FY2026 as sources/munis-ledgers/revenue/), which lists receipts by account and foots itself.

what: Does FY2024's debt service include the Mass Water Pool 9 balloon payment, or not?
why: The FY2013 annual town report's debt repayment schedule (PDF pages 81-82) prints, in its 2024 column, GRAND TOTAL PRINCIPAL 846,635 and GRAND TOTAL INTEREST 120,310 -- 966,945 -- against a printed TOTAL DEBT of 548,241. The document is out by 418,704 in that one column, and by the same 418,704 in its own TOTAL column (24,298,664 + 7,307,840 = 31,606,504 against a printed 31,187,800). Every other year of the 34 closes exactly. The figures were read off the page's own 400 dpi bitmap twice. 418,704 is also the principal the FY2014 annual report prints for `MASS WATER POOL 9*` in the FY2024 column -- the only row in that report's 156-row schedule with a principal and NO interest and NO total beside it (sources/data/page-reads/fy2014-p40-debt-schedule.csv). So the discrepancy is located on one borrowing, and it is still not known whether the town excludes that payment from debt service on purpose because the Trust subsidises it, or whether one of the two printed figures is simply wrong. The difference matters: it is 76% of what the town otherwise shows itself owing in FY2024. The per-issue rows of the FY2013 schedule are NOT read -- that limit is already registered as “What does each individual debt issue cost the town in a given year” and is not refiled here. — closes: the Treasurer's debt service schedule for the Mass Water Pollution Abatement Trust loan numbered 9, showing the FY2024 payment and any Trust subsidy against it.

what: What did Lunenburg owe, by borrowing and by fiscal year, from FY2020 to FY2035?
why: FY2019 PDF pages 49-52 print the whole forward debt repayment schedule -- about seventeen named borrowings against sixteen fiscal-year columns, each printed as PRINCIPAL / INTEREST / ADMIN FEE under a TOTAL row, on the order of 800 cells. It is fully self-proving (PRINCIPAL + INTEREST + ADMIN FEE = TOTAL, per issue per year, roughly 270 independent assertions). None of it has been read: `debt-repayment-detail-refused.csv` records 3 issue rows on p50 and 5 on p52 and no closing block, because the column header band at the top of each page sits inside the top 22.7% that the clipped render discarded. So the town's own forward debt service for sixteen years is published and unread. - closes: nothing from the Town is needed. The pages are legible at 150 dpi; this closes by reading them, after the document is re-OCR'd with the current renderer so the header band is visible. RESOLVED 2 October 2026: read in full, and the sizing in this row was wrong in every figure — it is FIFTEEN borrowings not seventeen, TWENTY-EIGHT fiscal years plus a TOTAL column not sixteen, 879 printed figures not ~800, and 213 issue-year identities not ~270. Measured off the pages. 198 of 213 close exactly and the 15 that miss by $1 are every one of them a Mass Water Pool trust line, which is displayed-dollar rounding and not a misread: bond principal, the column with no cents beneath it, ties exactly for 13 of 15 issues and the fifteen printed issue principals sum to $46,568,549 at ZERO tolerance.

what: What did each of the ~130 individual receipt lines on the FY2019 receipts page bring in?
why: PDF page 30 of the FY2019 annual town report (printed folio 28), `FY 2019 RECEIPTS - JUNE 2019`, prints about 130 named receipt lines in three label/amount column pairs, and separately a nine-category `SUMMARY OF RECEIPTS` with a GRAND TOTAL. The SUMMARY is now read and closes to the printed GRAND TOTAL of $40,734,004.07 to the cent (`sources/data/page-reads/fy2019-p30-receipts.csv`). THE DETAIL IS NOT READ. The page is a ~150 dpi photograph with no text layer, and recognition finds only about 75 of the ~130 printed money figures, so the second identity the page states about itself -- that the detail lines also sum to the GRAND TOTAL -- is untested. Until it is, FY2019 has category subtotals and no line-level receipts, so questions like what the town took in from building permits or from ambulance billing cannot be answered for that year from this page. - closes: nothing from the Town is needed and no better scan is required; the page is legible. This closes by transcribing the three column pairs and footing them to the nine category subtotals already proven, which is about 130 figures against ten independent assertions.

what: Which figure did the 2019 Annual Town Meeting vote for Central Purchasing, where the printed FY 2020 Omnibus Budget prints two that are a factor of ten apart?
why: The budget is printed on pages 161-164 of the FY2019 annual town report (printed pages 159-162) and the document contradicts itself in two places. p162 prints `38 Central Purchasing $ 603,030.00` and, three rows beneath it, `Total Central Purchasing $ 60,303.00` -- $542,727.00 apart. And p162 prints four Fire lines (1,093,374.24 + 20,000.00 + 15,000.00 + 10,000.00 = 1,138,374.24) above `Subtotal Fire Dept. $1,138,434.24`, $60.00 more than its own lines. Sixteen of the eighteen printed group totals foot their own line items to the cent and the twelve section totals sum to the printed `Total Omnibus $38,058,164.30` exactly, so this is the town's arithmetic and not our reading: both pairs were read at 400 dpi off the page's own bitmap. The town's grand total is footed on $60,303.00 and on $1,138,434.24, so the printed Total Omnibus cannot distinguish a misprinted line from a misprinted subtotal. A resident cannot tell from the published report what Central Purchasing was authorised to spend in FY2020, and the two readings differ by more than half a million dollars. -- closes: the Town Clerk's certified record of the vote on the FY2020 omnibus budget article at the 2019 Annual Town Meeting, with the schedule attached to the motion as moved.

what: Whether a board discussed a thing at a meeting it noticed but left no minutes and no recording of
why: 1,754 of the 6,990 meetings in sources/data/meeting-register.csv (25%) have a posted AGENDA and neither minutes nor a recording, so the only surviving record is that the meeting was noticed and what it meant to take up. 235 of them are since 1 July 2024. It is worst where a body is small: School Advisory Councils & Committees 229 of 268 (85%), Capital Planning 63 of 182 (35%), Board of Health 101 of 297 (34%). WHAT THIS IS NOT: it is not evidence that nothing was discussed, and a search that returns nothing for one of these dates has not searched the meeting -- it has searched an agenda. The practical cost is the inverse question. Parks Commission can be shown DISCUSSING its budget (44 of 192 meeting dates carry the word, and `Budget / Finance Review` is a named agenda item from 22 July 2026), and cannot be shown NOT to have, because 40 of its 193 meetings left no account at all -- including 30 September 2026, whose agenda item was `Budget Check-in`. This is distinct from the register's own limit, that a meeting with no agenda either is indistinguishable from one never held: here the town has published a notice, so the meeting is established and only its content is missing. — closes: the minutes themselves. G.L. c.30A §22 requires a public body to create and maintain accurate minutes of every meeting and to make them available on request, so for each of these dates the document is owed whether or not it was ever posted to the AgendaCenter. Requested by board and date.

what: Why the school department's FY2024 actual spending differs between its period 13 ledger and the general fund history, on 12 of 265 lines
why: Measured 5 October 2026 from the Finance Committee files: the period 13 report (`glytdbud`, generated 7 August 2024) and the FY2010-FY2025 general fund history agree to the cent on 253 of 265 school general-fund lines; 12 differ, by a net 243,636.29, the history higher -- led by a paraprofessional line and a clerical salary line, with some lines moving the other way. Entries posted to FY2024 after 7 August 2024 would produce this pattern; nothing here tests that. — closes: the Town Accountant's FY2024 journal entries posted after 7 August 2024 for fund 0100, department 300.

what: What a level-service budget for each town department would have cost, year by year
why: The general fund history the Finance Committee supplied holds each department’s original budget, transfers, revised budget and actual spending, FY2010–FY2025, and no request: nothing in it says what a department asked for or what keeping its service level would have cost. The schools present a level-service budget, and its difference from the appropriation is what is reported as the school deficit. For the town’s departments no equivalent figure is in this archive for any year before FY2027 — the year the Town Manager asked department heads for level-service budgets (Finance Committee minutes, 12 February 2026) and the override questions covered town and school alike — so whether they would have shown a gap in earlier years cannot be measured, and the difference between the two sides may be one of process rather than of cost. — closes: each town department’s budget request as submitted to the Town Manager, with the Town Manager’s recommendation beside it, for each fiscal year, held by the Town Manager’s office.

what: What the money was that reached departments’ revised budgets outside any recorded transfer
why: In the general fund history the revised budget differs from original plus transfers in and out on about one account-year in twenty, almost always upward, in every year FY2010–FY2025, and the workbook’s own Grand Total shows the same gap. By dollars, most of it is no larger than what the same account left unspent the year before, which is what a carried-forward encumbrance would look like; the rest fits a supplemental appropriation at a special Town Meeting. Neither is confirmed, and the difference matters: a carry-forward is last year’s money, a supplemental appropriation is new money. Measured in /analysis/department-budgets. — closes: the MUNIS budget amendment detail for each fiscal year, or the Town Accountant’s appropriations schedule with its APPROPRIATED FORWARD column, which the annual report printed through FY2023.

what: Whether a town department’s budget growth is more service or a cost moved into it from another budget
why: Several town departments’ starting budgets grew in single steps — general highway maintenance, facilities and grounds, public buildings and recycling each have one year in which the starting budget rose by more than a third — and a step that size fits a service being taken on, or a cost moved in from another line or fund, as well as it fits the same service costing more. The ledger records dollars by account and nothing about why an account moved, so a growth rate measured across such a step is not a trend. Measured in /analysis/department-budgets. — closes: the Town Manager’s budget message, or the Finance Committee’s report to Town Meeting, for each year in which a department’s starting budget stepped.

what: Why the general fund’s starting budget grew more slowly than the levy limit, FY2010 to FY2025
why: Measured from the general fund history against the Division of Local Services’ certified levy limits, the whole starting budget grew more slowly each year, on average, than the levy limit did — even with the FY2025 override taken back out of the limit. Three readings fit: the rest of the revenue (state aid, local receipts, free cash) grew more slowly than the levy; the town levied below its limit; or money raised under the limit went outside the general fund operating budget, to capital articles or enterprise subsidies. They imply different things about how much room the levy has left. Measured in /analysis/department-budgets. — closes: the Tax Rate Recapitulation for each fiscal year, which states the levy actually raised, the excess levy capacity and every other source the budget was balanced with.

what: Where did the $122,502.44 that moved out of the FY2025 school department mid-year go, and what posted to department 300 after the School Committee's 17 September 2025 surplus statement?
why: The closed MUNIS ledger (sources/data/munis-school-ytd.csv, FY2025 period 13, department 300) carries transfers_adjustments as a net figure per account, with no counterparty -- so a line moved in cannot be matched to the line it moved out of. And the ledger's own $627,116.86 available at the close exceeds the $603,885.97 the district reported that day by $23,230.89, with no single account or pair of accounts equal to the gap, which is consistent with activity posted after 17 September 2025 but not established by anything held here. — closes: the FY2025 transfer schedule for department 300 with counterparties and authority, and the journal entries posted to department 300 after 17 September 2025.

what: How many children enter or leave an out-of-district placement during a school year, and when?
why: Only two snapshots are published, months apart and taken by different bodies: DESE's count of students with disabilities placed out of district in October, and the town's count of placements on 1 March in the Special Services report of each annual town report. Their difference is a NET change -- an arrival and a departure between the two dates cancel, and a child placed and returned between them is in neither -- and some of it may be the two bodies counting differently. DESE's caseload-movement file (8aww-sugs) counts children entering and leaving special education SERVICES, not placements. The district has said at public meetings that children have moved in already needing a placement and that a child entering after 1 April is the sending district's cost; neither is a count. A mid-year reserve for tuition is sized by exactly this number, which is why /analysis/special-education-costs cannot size one from children and sizes it from the ledger instead. — closes: the district's out-of-district placement log, one row per placement with its start date, end date and setting (collaborative, day or residential) and no names, from the Director of Student Services by records request.

what: What does one out-of-district placement cost Lunenburg in a year?
why: DESE publishes what the district spent on tuition to private schools and collaboratives (functions 9300 and 9400), by fund, and the town publishes how many children were placed on 1 March. Nothing in this archive prices a single placement. /analysis/special-education-costs divides the first by the second and labels the result our estimate; /what-special-education-costs refuses to, and both are right about what the quotient is not: it mixes residential, day and collaborative places, it counts a child placed for part of a year as either a whole year or nothing depending on one day, and transportation is in a different line. A reserve for an unplanned placement needs the price of one, and the only figure available is that estimate. — closes: the accounts-payable detail behind general fund and fund 2640 accounts in functions 9300 and 9400 -- vendor, invoice period and amount, no student names -- from the Town Accountant, or the district's tuition rate sheets for the year.

what: Does segment 51 of a school account string mean special education?
why: The town's account string is nine segments; the fourth is the DESE function code. The fifth is 51 on every general fund school account whose own description names special education, except special education transportation, and /analysis/special-education-costs classifies in-district special education by it -- less two accounts the district's own budget book labels as English learner costs, which shows the segment is not purely special education. The meaning of the segment is read from the account names, not from a published chart of accounts, so the in-district total rests on our reading. — closes: the Town's MUNIS chart of accounts, with the definition of each segment and its values, from the Town Accountant.

what: How much the Special Education Reserve Fund holds, and what the law lets it do
why: Special Town Meeting on 18 November 2025 accepted Mass. General Laws chapter 40 section 13E and established a Special Education Reserve Fund for unanticipated or unbudgeted special education, out-of-district tuition and transportation costs (FY2025 annual town report). The Town Manager told the Select Board on 7 October 2025 that spending from it needs a majority of both the School Committee and the Select Board and that its balance may not exceed 2% of annual net school spending. The statute itself is not in this archive, so the cap and the vote are as described at a meeting; and no balance, deposit or withdrawal is in any ledger held here. The School Committee's agenda for 7 October 2026 carries an item to vote an amount to fund it. — closes: the text of chapter 40 section 13E (malegislature.gov, public); and the Treasurer's balance of the fund with every vote to fund or spend it, from the Town Accountant.

what: How much of the $236,766.94 still encumbered in the FY2026 school general fund at period 13 will be paid, how much released to the surplus, and how much carried into FY2027?
why: The FY2026 period-13 MUNIS report for department 300 (sources/data/munis-school-ytd.csv), run on 6 October 2026, shows $482,118.07 unspent and $236,766.94 still encumbered across 27 accounts -- the largest electricity ($62,362.13) and collaborative tuitions ($58,708.07). Between the period-12 run of 1 September 2026 and that run, spending did not move in any account and one encumbrance of $16.95 was released, so the FY26 school surplus is still anywhere from $482,118.07 to $718,885.01. The FY2025 report run the same day shows nothing encumbered. A ledger shows a commitment, not whether it will be paid, cancelled or carried forward, and which of those happens decides the surplus. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus. — closes: the FY2026 period-13 report for department 300 run again after the year-end close, and the Town Accountant's list of FY2026 encumbrances carried forward into FY2027, by account.

what: What was the School Committee told under "FY26 Year End Budget review" on 2 and 9 September 2026?
why: Both agendas carry the item (Old Business, 5 minutes). The archive's catalogue of the Town's AgendaCenter lists no minutes for either meeting, so the only written statement on the FY26 school year-end held here is the 29 July 2026 minutes, in which the business manager was "confident the remaining amount would be well below" the approximately $600,000 returned in FY25. The machine captions of the recordings can locate a moment but are not a record. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus. — closes: the approved School Committee minutes of 2 and 9 September 2026, and any year-end budget document presented under that item.

what: Why does DESE's FY2024 figure for out-of-district tuition paid from funds other than the general fund exceed what the circuit breaker account paid by exactly the FY2024 circuit breaker payment?
why: DESE's End of Year Financial Report reports FY2024 tuition (functions 9300 and 9400) paid from funds other than the general fund. The town's year-end report for the school special funds shows what the circuit breaker account (fund 2640) paid in tuition that year. The remainder between the two is, to the dollar, the circuit breaker payment DESE's reimbursement file lists for FY2024; in FY2023 and FY2025 the remainder is small. The figures are computed, not typed, in the report's payload under circuit_breaker.unexplained. It may be a coincidence, a second fund, or the receipt reported as an expenditure; nothing in this archive distinguishes them, so /analysis/special-education-costs shows the figure as 'other funds' and says it cannot explain it. Computed in scripts/build_sped_costs.py, which refuses to print the sentence if the equality stops holding. — closes: the district's FY2024 End of Year Financial Report as submitted to DESE (Schedule 1 by fund), or the school special funds year-end report for any fund other than 2640 that paid tuition in FY2024.

what: Was the FY2026 school surplus thrift — did discretionary spending slow late in the year?
why: A speaker at the School Committee on 7 October 2026 said, per our machine captions, "We were thrifty"; no posted minutes record a decision to hold FY2026 spending. The period-13 ledger shows where money was left (by our category table, 59% of it in supplies, upkeep and equipment) but only as year-end totals, so restraint, a postponed project and a line budgeted high look identical. The school journal by month is now held, and it shows WHEN: spending fell behind its usual pace from February (40.2% of the budget left at the end of March against about 33% in FY2023 and FY2024), and ten building payees used every year were paid under half as usual. It cannot show whether anyone DECIDED to hold spending. — closes: any written or minuted instruction in FY2026 to hold, defer or freeze school purchasing, with its date.

what: Which school counselor, social-worker and psychologist posts were vacant or on leave in FY2026, and for how long?
why: The FY2026 period-13 ledger leaves these salary lines well under budget — one psychologist account spent nothing of its budget — and no posted minutes explain it. A dollar is not a post (rule 11): vacancy, leave, a lower hiring step and contracted cover all produce the same row. One cause is on the record: on 29 July 2026 $81,075.96 moved off the high school special education resource room teacher line, and asked Was that an unfilled position?" the answer was "a leave of absence" (captions). Looking back

what: Why FY2026 private special-education tuition came in far under budget while collaborative tuition ran far over
why: In the FY2026 period-13 ledger the general fund’s private-tuition line (9300) ended well under budget and its collaborative-tuition line (9400) well over, netting to a small surplus; the circuit breaker fund (2640) paid collaborative tuition that year and no private tuition, the reverse of FY2025. Fewer private placements, placements moved to collaboratives, and the line a payment was charged to all fit the same rows. — closes: the FY2026 out-of-district placement list by setting, with start dates and each tuition invoice and the fund it was paid from.

what: What the town’s own special revenue funds held at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026
why: The annual town reports print every special revenue fund's balance at 30 June, and this project has read and proved FY2011 to FY2023 -- forward, receipts, disbursements and carried, every row and every printed GRAND TOTAL tying (special-revenue-read.csv). FY2024 and FY2025 print a DIFFERENT table, a balance detail with no receipts or disbursements, no row identity and no stable fund key: it is printed and has not yet been read into a dataset, which is our gap rather than the town's. FY2026's annual report is not yet published. The school side of 'is anyone sitting on money' runs to 30 June 2026 through the MUNIS period-13 ledgers; the town side stops at 30 June 2023, so whether the town's own funds kept growing cannot be said. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: a MUNIS fund balance report (or trial balance) at period 13 for FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 covering the town's special revenue funds -- the same system that produced the school delivery of 6 October 2026, pointed at the town's funds.

what: What the school grant funds held at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026
why: Fourteen school funds -- circuit breaker, school choice, lunch, eight fee-funded revolving funds and three gift funds -- are carried from the annual report's 30 June 2023 balance through the MUNIS period-13 ledgers, and the result ties to the cent to the Town's March 2026 special revenue report for every one. The grant funds cannot be carried that way: the annual report names a grant by programme and year, MUNIS numbers it, and nothing published maps one to the other; and a reimbursement grant spends before it is paid, so one year's revenue less expense is not a change in what it holds. So the school total after 2023 covers the fourteen and not the grants. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: a MUNIS fund balance report at period 13 for the school grant funds (26xx-29xx), FY2024 to FY2026, with each fund's opening and closing balance.

what: Why local receipts come in above the town’s own estimate
why: The state's free cash proof shows receipts above the town's estimate (its line CL#6) as one of the largest components of Lunenburg's free cash in every one of the five years it covers, and above a million dollars in four of them. On 28 May 2026 a Finance Committee member told the committee the town had not collected less than four million dollars in local receipts in ten years, against a current estimate of 3.535 million. Three readings fit the same line: an estimate set low on purpose as a buffer; receipts that grew faster than any forecast could know; or one-time receipts that should not be estimated at all. They imply different things about how much of each year's free cash is predictable, and so about how much the budget could count on. Measured in /analysis/sitting-on-money. — closes: the town's local receipts estimate against actual collections, by category, for each year -- the local receipts page of each year's Tax Rate Recapitulation beside DLS Schedule A.

what: How much of the special education circuit breaker account's balance is already committed to the next year's tuition?
why: The account (fund 2640) pays out-of-district tuition every year, overrun or not, and its 30 June balance is computed on /analysis/special-education-costs and /analysis/sitting-on-money. Whether that balance is free to meet a mid-year surprise, or is already planned against next year's placements, is not published: the year-end ledgers show what was spent, not what was intended, and in one year the account carried a tuition budget while in the others it carried none. So a resident cannot tell how much of the balance is a cushion beside the new special education reserve. — closes: the district's circuit breaker spending plan for the year, or the budget narrative for the out-of-district tuition line stating how much it assumes the account will pay.

what: Which school special revenue funds the period-13 special funds report leaves out
why: The FY2023 annual town report's special revenue schedule prints $3,667,636 received and $4,333,280 spent across every school special revenue fund; the MUNIS period-13 special funds report for the same year, delivered 6 October 2026, carries $2,440,883 and $2,962,716. The difference is funds that report does not carry -- among them, the annual report's FY22 ESSER II #115, FY22 ARP Idea #252 and FY22 Idea ARP #264 rows have no fund of that name or number in the MUNIS report. And the FY2026 report books $59,333 of grant revenue against $557,427 of grant spending. A reimbursement booked after the close, a grant receipt held in a fund outside the report, and both together all fit; the report cannot separate them, so whether the schools spend the grant money that comes in can be said only for the funds it carries. Measured in /analysis/spending-what-comes-in. — closes: the MUNIS period-13 revenue and expense report for EVERY school special revenue fund, FY2023 to FY2026, with each fund's opening and closing balance (or the trial balance for funds 2xxx at each close).

what: What a fee-funded school programme costs that is not booked to its own fund
why: A revolving fund that takes in more than it spends covers the costs BOOKED TO IT, and nothing more (rule 11). The ledger can test whether the general fund also carries a programme's costs only where both book to the same programme-specific DESE function code, and among the schools' fee and lunch funds that is true of athletics alone (function 3510, where the general fund booked most of the four years' athletics spending). Extended day, after-school activities, facilities rental and adult education book their spending to function codes that name no programme -- 2000, 4000, 5200 -- so whether the general fund pays any of their custodians, utilities, administration or benefits cannot be shown either way. 'Pays its own way' therefore cannot be stated for any of them beyond their own books. Measured in /analysis/spending-what-comes-in. — closes: the district's indirect-cost allocation for each revolving programme, or a cost study listing the general fund accounts that carry part of each programme's cost.

what: What was paid from the school budget lines that spent against a $0 budget, FY2023–FY2026
why: The closed MUNIS ledger (sources/data/munis-school-ytd.csv, report gf-school, period 13) gives one spent figure per account per year and nothing else: not the payee, not the warrant, not whether it was salary for a person or a coding correction. /analysis/spent-with-no-budget lists every general fund line that spent against a $0 voted budget; for every one of them, what the money bought is unknown. — closes: a MUNIS general ledger detail (journal) export for department 300, FY2023–FY2026, for those accounts, with the warrant or payroll reference on each entry.

what: Whether the FY2026 spending on the kindergarten aide lines paid for aides in kindergarten classrooms
why: The ledger books FY2026 spending to two accounts titled kindergarten aides and kindergarten paraprofessionals (orgs S2032121 and S2032131), both voted at $0; a Finance Committee minute of 12 January 2026 records the School Committee chair saying kindergarten classrooms had no aides. An account title is not a person in a room: staff coded to the line while assigned elsewhere, a reclassification, or posts moved between lines all print the same ledger, and nothing published joins the account to a building. — closes: the FY2026 payroll distribution for the two accounts, naming position and building (names may be redacted).

what: What the Dee Bus rates and fleet were in FY2025, so the 7.6% FY2026 increase can be split into price and buses
why: The FY2026 budget's "7.6% line increase = $69,300" is exactly the new contract's first-year regular-route price ($976,500: 8 buses at $485 and 3 at $515 a day, 180 days) over the FY2025 budget line ($907,200). The new contract fixes every year's price per bus per day, so FY2027 and FY2028 are known; the FY2025 side is one number, $907,200, which fits eleven buses at an average $458.18 a day (all of the 7.6% is price) and ten at $504.00 (the increase is a bus, not price) equally well. A district presentation says 11 buses were in use; that is a statement, not a rate. Requested on 9 October 2026 and not delivered. See notes/findings/DEE-BUS-CONTRACT.md. — closes: the FY2023-FY2025 Dee Bus contract and its bid form (daily price per bus by size, number of buses), or the FY2025 Dee Bus invoices.

what: What the corrected paraprofessional salary scale costs, and what was underpaid
why: The School Committee approved a corrected paraprofessional scale on 7 October 2026: 107 of 120 hourly rates rose, steps 1-8 by about 4% (FY2026-FY2027) and 4.5% (FY2028), and the top steps did not move. Draft agreements released with it offer a lump sum of FY2027 retroactive pay and one personal day in exchange for a Wage Act waiver covering FY2026 and part of FY2027; the Superintendent's estimate is about 52 people. The cost cannot be computed: the scale is a full-year figure at 6.5 hours a day, and nothing published says how many paraprofessionals sit in each column and step or on what hours, nor what each was actually paid. See notes/findings/PARA-SALARY-CORRECTION.md. — closes: payroll's calculation of the FY2027 retroactive payment (headcount by column, step and appointed hours, with the sums), or the costing put to the School Committee for the 7 October vote.

what: How many athletic bus trips each sport took, and what each trip cost
why: The district's sport-by-sport workbook gives transportation dollars per sport for FY2024 to FY2026 as sums of charges, and the posted schedules (ArbiterLive) list each team's away games and venues from FY2022. /analysis/transportation prices the schedules at the Dee Bus contract's per-mile and per-hour rates as our estimate, with the waiting hours an assumption from the bid form. What no document shows is which games actually got a bus, whether teams shared one, how long each bus waited, and what each charge on the sheet was. — closes: the Dee Bus athletic and field-trip invoices for FY2024 to FY2026, with date, team, miles and waiting hours per trip, from the Business Office

what: Whether the school choice fund’s SCH. CHOICE BUS FEE account is where the student bus fees are booked
why: In the school special funds year-end reports, fund 1308 (school choice) carries revenue account 437601, SCH. CHOICE BUS FEE. It took in nothing in FY2023 and FY2024, began receiving money in FY2025 -- the year the first student bus fees fell due -- and received again in FY2026, while the town general fund's STUDENTBUS revenue account shows nothing. That timing fits the fees and does not establish them: the account is named for school choice, and a fee charged only to school choice students would book the same way. Narrows 'Where bus fee receipts are booked' without closing it. — closes: the Town Accountant's definition of account 1308-437601, or the cash receipts detail behind it for FY2025 and FY2026 showing whether the deposits are the RevTrak and check payments for the student bus fee.

what: How many vans, monitors and routes special education transportation pays for, and at what rates
why: The general fund special education transportation line is the only published figure: voted and spent, by year. The district's FY2026 budget overview attributes the line's rise to a rate increase and to more vans and monitors, and the August 2026 route list for the regular buses excludes the special education vans. The van contract is not in this archive, so price, routes, children and monitors cannot be separated, and no cost per child transported can be computed. — closes: the district's contract with Van Pool Transportation for special education transportation and its rate schedule, with the number of vans, routes and monitors by year; from the Business Office by records request.

what: How many children ride the school buses, and how many pay the fee
why: The only count in the record is the Superintendent's report to the School Committee on 4 June 2025 of bus requests received, and how many were unpaid, for the first fee year. A request is not a rider and an unpaid request is not a refusal. Without riders, no cost per rider and no share of the bus cost covered by the fee can be computed, and whether the fee changed ridership cannot be seen. — closes: the district's transportation registration count for each school year by grade band, fee tier (one child, family, reduced, free) and paid status, with the ridership counts the routes are planned on.

what: Why DESE’s FY2025 transportation spending for Lunenburg differs from the town ledger
why: DESE's End of Year Financial Report gives general fund in-district transportation (function 3300) and out-of-district transportation, and their sum equals the town's MUNIS regular plus special education transportation accounts to the dollar in FY2022, FY2023 and FY2024. In FY2025 DESE's sum is higher than the ledger and nothing published explains it. In FY2020 and FY2021 the two differ by equal and opposite amounts, which is what one payment booked in different years by the two would look like. — closes: the district's FY2025 End of Year Financial Report workpapers mapping MUNIS accounts to DESE functions, from the Business Office.

what: What the athletic fee fund held at each 30 June, FY2021 to FY2026
why: SETTLED IN PART, 28 October 2026. A year end is now printed for every year: the annual town reports' special revenue schedule, $189,410.67 (FY2021), $296,286.42 (FY2022) and $126,372.26 (FY2023); the FY2024 report's Special Revenue Fund Balance Detail, page 23, $11,562.99; the FY2025 report's same schedule, $131,239.09; and the district's own FY2026 reconciliation (school-funds-fy26.xlsx, a sheet the district assembled), $152,280.91 at 30 June 2026. They are not one basis. The FY2025 figure is the fund's cash -- the cashbook closes FY2025 at the same cent -- and is $20,991.20 above the $110,247.89 fund balance the district file opens FY2026 with; that file calls the gap accounts payable but dates it 6/30/26, while the journal shows it paid on 8 July 2025. By our running total of the cashbook, the fund's cash went below zero inside FY2024 and FY2025 (lowest -$117,947.62, 21 March 2025) before journal entries moved costs onto the town budget. Still open: a year end the Town itself states on one basis for FY2024 to FY2026, with what was owed shown apart from cash. Shown on /athletics/fee-fund-history. — closes: the Town Accountant's fund 1301 balance sheet at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026 (the MUNIS balance sheet report, period 13), showing cash, accounts payable and fund balance separately.

what: What the athletic fee fund’s high school purchase-of-service account paid for in FY2026
why: Account 1301-3-300-3510-06-0-00-2-531006, where athletic buses were charged before they moved to the general fund, books officials, ice time, dues and transportation together. In FY2026 -- the first year the general fund athletic transportation line was budgeted to carry the full cost of athletic buses -- it spent about as much as in FY2024, when it still carried most of them. Fits equally: officials, ice time or other costs rose; some buses are still charged to the fund; reclassifications landed in a different year. Nothing published separates them. — closes: the accounts-payable detail for fund 1301 account 531006, FY2024 to FY2026, by vendor and invoice, from the Town Accountant.

what: Why FY2024’s regular-route bus spending was higher than FY2025’s
why: The general fund regular-route transportation account spent more in FY2024 than in FY2025, and closed FY2024 past its revised budget even after a transfer in, while FY2025 spent its budget exactly. Both years were under the Dee Bus contract that preceded the current one, which this archive does not hold, so whether FY2024 carried an extra bus, extra routes, a price step that later reversed, or a cost booked in the wrong year cannot be told. A Finance Committee member asked for the bus contracts in March 2024. — closes: the Dee Bus contract in force for FY2024 and FY2025 with its rate schedule, and the FY2024 Dee Bus invoices (the contract was requested on 9 October 2026).

what: Will the school accounts that closed FY2026 past their revised budgets be covered by year-end transfers, and from which lines?
why: The FY2026 period-13 MUNIS report for department 300 (sources/data/munis-school-ytd.csv, run 6 October 2026) shows 57 accounts past their revised budgets by $1,201,433.81, after the ten year-end transfers the School Committee approved on 29 July 2026 ($148,364.31), whose minutes say more "may still be forthcoming". FY2025 closed with 4 such accounts; FY2023 with 70 and FY2024 with 52. The school appropriation is a bottom-line total, so this is not spending past the appropriation; it is whether the line budgets the next budget is built from say where the money goes. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus — closes: the FY2026 year-end line-item transfer schedule for department 300 as posted, by account, with the vote that authorised each.

what: What does the FY2027 out-of-district tuition budget assume: which placements, for which months, and how much the circuit breaker will pay?
why: The district's FY2027 workbook (budget-workbooks/fy27-proposals.xlsx) budgets $700,142 across private and collaborative tuition, the same figure in every scenario. The same two general-fund lines spent and committed $1,202,770.94 in FY2026 at period 13, and the circuit breaker fund (2640) paid $333,494.89 more. Placements ending, a larger circuit-breaker share, or FY2027 tuition paid in advance out of FY2026 money all fit, and the ledger cannot tell them apart. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus — closes: the FY2027 tuition worksheet (each placement anonymised: setting, rate, months, and the fund expected to pay it) and the service period of every FY2026 tuition invoice.

what: Where did each FY2026 school line-item transfer come from, and where did it go?
why: The MUNIS year-to-date report gives one NET transfer figure per account, so a line that gave and received money in the same year shows only the difference. The 29 July 2026 School Committee minutes record $11,000 moved out of natural-gas heating; the ledger shows heating up $11,024.22, net. The 5 November 2025 minutes record $13,500 moved to School Committee dues "to cover superintendent search invoice"; that line closed FY2026 with $13,689 unspent and had spent less than its original budget. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus — closes: the MUNIS budget transfer report for department 300, FY2026, gross, with each entry's date and counterparty account.

what: Why has school electricity run past its voted budget in every year from FY2023 to FY2026?
why: Account 0100-3-300-4130-99-1-74-2-521011 spent and committed $303,101.82 more than it was voted across FY2023-FY2026, and the FY2027 budget, $316,250, is below the $319,108.72 FY2026 had already paid. Natural-gas heating beside it was voted above its spending in FY2024-FY2026 and received transfers in every year. Usage, rates, load moving from gas to electricity, and the solar panels a Finance Committee member asked about on 26 February 2026 all fit. /analysis/fy26-school-surplus — closes: the school utility bills by building and month, with kilowatt-hours and any solar or net-metering credit.

what: Whether the FY2025 spring section of the district’s by-sport athletics workbook is complete
why: The district's sport-by-sport workbook prints $0.00 as its FY2025 spring season total, in cell AT25, while its spring rows sum to $18,242.50, 46.1% below FY2024's spring rows; spring is 58.9% of the whole fall in athletic transportation from FY2024 to FY2025. Outdoor track, baseball, softball and lacrosse all look cheaper in FY2025 on that sheet, and /analysis/transportation cannot say whether that is fewer or shorter trips or a section filled in before the season's bills arrived. Every other season total the workbook prints equals its own rows. — closes: the district's confirmation that the FY2025 spring transportation column is final, or Dee Bus's spring 2025 athletic invoices, from the Business Office.

what: Which budget lines the School Committee's line item transfers moved, when the minutes record only the vote
why: Of the transfers the School Committee approved in the minutes read so far (every set the archive holds, 6 September 2023 to 26 August 2026), some are recorded only as a vote to approve transfers "as outlined" or "as presented", or as one total for a batch, with no from-line, to-line or amount -- 24 June 2026 approved four transfers with no figure printed, and 4 October 2023 approved $127,786 as a single total. The minutes are the record of the VOTE; the lines are on the district's transfer sheet the committee is shown, and the archive holds that sheet for only three: 26 September 2025 (the athletic $20,000), 5-6 October 2026 (FY2027) and one from October 2022. The recordings cannot substitute: a caption model hears figures unreliably. And the town's ledger extracts held here carry no budget-transfer journal for the school department, so nothing can tie a vote to the accounts it moved. — closes: the line item transfer sheets presented at each School Committee meeting (in the meeting packets), or the MUNIS budget transfer journal for the school department, by fiscal year.

what: Which of the people on the school district's master staff list still work for the district
why: The district publishes its staff two ways: a sheet per building, and one master list ("Directory of Staff - All Lunenburg Public Schools Staff", a published Google Sheet). They disagree. On the 9 October 2026 fetch, 36 people appear on the master list at a building that keeps its own sheet -- 25 at the Primary School, 10 at Turkey Hill, 1 at the High School -- and that building's own sheet does not list them; a resident who knows the schools reports that at least one of them left years ago. The org chart takes each building's own sheet as the authority and sets those 36 aside, named, on the chart; it keeps 11 people the master list places district-wide or at the shared Middle/High building, marked as on that list alone. Neither list says which is current, and neither carries a start or end date. — closes: the district's current staff roster from Human Resources (or the MUNIS payroll employee list), dated.

what: Which games Lunenburg’s athletic teams played in the seasons their posted schedules do not cover
why: /analysis/transportation builds its athletic bus model from the schedules the district posts on ArbiterLive, the scheduling site linked from its athletics page. ArbiterLive lists only what a coach posts: cheer posts no schedule at all, some teams post none in some years, and indoor and outdoor track list far fewer meets than the district's by-sport sheet has charges. A team with no listed game is not a team that took no bus, so the model is a floor for those teams and cannot be checked against the sheet for them. — closes: the athletic department's final game and meet schedule for each team, FY2022 to FY2026, with home and away and the venue, from the Athletic Director by records request.

what: How the district built its FY2027 athletic transportation estimate
why: On 26 August 2026 the Superintendent put restoring high school athletic buses at about $58,880, attributing the lower figure to scheduling competitions closer to Lunenburg, more home competitions, and estimating from actual schedules and prior-year spring costs. /analysis/transportation tests the first two reasons against the posted schedules and prices the schedules with the contract's rates, but most of its result is the hours a bus waits, which is an assumption. Without the worksheet behind the estimate, the two cannot be set side by side assumption for assumption. — closes: the worksheet or calculation behind the $58,880 FY2027 athletic transportation estimate (trips, miles and waiting hours by team), from the Superintendent's office.

what: How many votes each FY2027 override question received on 16 May 2026
why: Two records disagree and neither is the certified count. The Town's unofficial tally sheet (town-supplementary/docs/town-2026-election-unofficial-results.pdf) foots precinct by precinct to its own ballots-cast total; the Division of Local Services' override record prints different yes and no counts for both questions, whose yes plus no alone exceed that ballots-cast total. Which is right is not established here. — closes: the Town Clerk's certified results of the 16 May 2026 Annual Town Election.

what: Which accounts Lunenburg's FY2025 health insurance figure on the state's Schedule A counts
why: The state's figure for Lunenburg equals the town insurance department less Medicare and life insurance in every year FY2010-FY2023, and the whole department in FY2024 (asserted in scripts/build_health_insurance_topics.py). So any growth rate measured across FY2024 mixes a change in what was counted with a change in spending, and FY2025 cannot be tied because the ledger history's FY2025 actuals are part-year. — closes: the town's FY2025 Schedule A health insurance detail, set against the year-end ledger.

what: How much of Monty Tech’s FY2026 spending is outside its operating budget, and from which funds
why: The district’s FY 2027 Budget Summary sets out its operating (general fund) budget for FY2026 and FY2027 and the five sources that pay for it: Chapter 70, the member towns’ assessments, state transportation aid, its Regional Transportation Fund and its Excess & Deficiency reserve. Grants and revolving funds are not in it. DESE’s expenditures-by-function file DOES split the district’s total by fund, general fund against grants and revolving, but only through FY2025, and that total, which DESE titles Expenditure (Admin, Instruction, Operations), carries no capital or debt service row. So the operating budget on /enrolment/monty-tech-funding and DESE’s per-pupil figure are different years and different scopes, and nothing here reconciles them. — closes: DESE’s End of Year Financial Report for LEA 08320000 for FY2026, which splits spending by fund.

what: Do two districts put the same purchase on the same side of the line, so that their per-pupil figures compare like for like?
why: DESE’s per-pupil figure counts functions 1000-5000 and leaves out capital (7000) and debt service (8000); its expenditures-by-function file carries no 6000, 7000 or 8000 row for any district, so no district’s figure contains capital. But the line between counted and capital is a coding rule, and DESE’s FY2025 End of Year Report form draws it: instructional equipment, “including vocational equipment and science lab equipment irrespective of unit cost”, goes in 2420 and is counted; non-instructional equipment over $5,000 and extraordinary maintenance over $150,000 a project go in 7000 and are not. Whether every district applies that rule the same way cannot be seen: DESE publishes each district’s reported totals, not the purchases behind them. So a difference between two districts on an equipment or maintenance line may be spending, or may be coding. — closes: each district’s own End of Year Financial Report workbook with its 7000 schedule, lease schedule and depreciation schedule, and DESE’s desk-review or audit findings on them.

what: How much of DESE’s general fund figure for Lunenburg the school budget paid, and how much other town budgets paid
why: DESE’s per-pupil figure counts general fund spending on the schools whoever paid it: insurance for retired school staff (function 5250) is in it, and in FY2026 the town carries that insurance in its own insurance department (SCHRETHLTH), not in the school appropriation. DESE’s expenditures-by-function file has one GEN_FUND column and does not say which budget paid which line, so the school appropriation divided by pupils is not DESE’s figure a pupil, and the difference cannot be itemised from it. Found building /school-spending/per-pupil-line-by-line. — closes: the district’s End of Year Financial Report as filed with DESE, whose Schedule 1 reports expenditures by the school committee and, separately, expenditures by city or town (part B, row 1016 of DESE’s FY2025 form), for the same year.

what: How much of Harvard’s higher spending a pupil comes from being a smaller district
why: Harvard spends more a pupil than Lunenburg on DESE’s all-funds measure, and divides its spending among fewer pupils. A smaller district spreads costs that do not shrink with enrolment — a principal, a building, a superintendent’s office — over fewer pupils, so part of any per-pupil gap may be scale rather than programme, and DESE’s function-code file cannot say how much: it reports dollars by function, not which costs are fixed. The Bromfield shelf states this as a hypothesis and tests nothing. — closes: nothing published settles it; DESE’s staffing by job classification and salary (EPIMS) for both districts, school by school, would bound the share that is fixed posts.

what: What part of Lunenburg’s Monty Tech assessment the property tax levy pays, rather than state aid or other receipts
why: A member town pays its regional assessment out of one budget that the levy, Chapter 70 and local receipts fund together, and no document assigns one revenue to one appropriation. So /homes-and-taxes/regional-school-share can only ESTIMATE the assessment’s weight in an average bill, in proportion to its share of the levy (our arithmetic on DLS values and rates by class). For the other seventeen member towns only the state-required minimum is held, not the whole assessment. — closes: nothing assigns it; the town’s tax recapitulation sheet sets every appropriation against the levy and every receipt, and each member town’s voted Monty Tech appropriation would replace the minimum.

what: Why the state’s FY2011 teacher count for Lunenburg dips and recovers a year later
why: DESE’s teacher file and its comparison sheet both print the FY2011 figure, and the fall shows at every one of the four schools, so it is not one school left out of the return. The state’s own total fell more that year than in any other year it publishes, which fits real cuts; but Lunenburg’s fall is among the largest in the state, and three of the four schools read higher again in FY2012. The file cannot tell a reduction restored a year later from a reporting error, so any comparison that starts in FY2011 measures the file as much as the staff. See /school-spending-history/fy2011-teacher-reading — closes: Lunenburg’s EPIMS teacher assignments by school for FY2011, or the district’s own staffing list for that school year.

what: How many teachers Lunenburg employed before FY2008
why: Net school spending and the 1 October enrolment count are published from FY1994; DESE’s teacher file starts with FY2008 and the town’s printed school rosters with FY2011, and a roster carries no FTE. So the first part of the long-run comparison on /school-spending-history has spending and pupils and no teachers beside them, and the teacher line can only be drawn from FY2008 — closes: any DESE staffing report for Lunenburg before FY2008, or the district’s own staffing history by year.

what: What school spending has been in constant dollars
why: CLOSED 18 October 2026. The Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI-U for Boston-Cambridge-Newton (series CUURS11ASA0, January 1990 onward) is landed in sources/federal-bls/, four API responses saved as returned with their addresses and sha256, and its PROVENANCE.md says how the fiscal-year average is built. Every spending page on /school-spending-history now gives dollars as printed beside dollars of the latest actual year, July-June averages, our arithmetic. What the index does NOT settle: it measures what a basket of consumer goods costs in the Boston area, not what a school pays for teachers, tuition or insurance, so "after prices" means after general prices -- closes: the CPI-U for Boston-Cambridge-Newton, landed; for a school-specific measure, the state and local government price deflator the state uses to inflate the Chapter 70 foundation budget.

what: How many of Lunenburg’s teachers sit on each step and lane of the salary schedule, each year?
why: DESE’s Teachers function grew while teacher FTE fell, so spending per teacher FTE rose. An average moves with raises, with teachers moving up steps and lanes, and with who is on staff (fewer, more senior teachers raise it with nobody’s pay changing), and DESE publishes no count by step or lane, so the three cannot be told apart. See /school-spending-history/pay-or-headcount. — closes: the district’s count of teachers on each step and lane of the salary schedule, for each year.

what: What raises did Lunenburg’s teachers’ agreements give before FY2025?
why: The only teachers’ agreement held is the one running 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2027 (sources/contracts/), so the schedule adjustments behind the rise in spending per teacher from FY2009 to FY2024 are not known. — closes: the Lunenburg Education Association agreements before the current one, from the district or as filed with DESE.

what: What are the current teacher salary schedules in Groton-Dunstable, Ayer Shirley, Leominster and Ashburnham-Westminster?
why: NARROWED 19 October 2026. The current agreements of Lunenburg, Harvard, North Middlesex, Fitchburg and Montachusett are held and their salary schedules read cell by cell (sources/data/teacher-salary-schedules.csv); on those five FY2026 schedules Lunenburg’s bachelor’s and master’s top steps are the lowest, before longevity, which every contract but Harvard’s pays outside the grid. For these four districts the only contracts held are the ones DESE publishes, and each has expired: Groton-Dunstable’s schedules run 2017-18 to 2019-20, Ayer Shirley’s 2019-20 to 2021-22, Leominster’s 2015-16 to 2017-18 and Ashburnham-Westminster’s 2016-17 to 2018-19. So three of the project’s six comparison districts cannot be compared on pay scale for any current year. See /school-spending-history/teacher-pay-compared. — closes: each district’s current Unit A teachers’ agreement, with its salary schedules, by records request.

what: What does DESE count as an “experienced” teacher in its teacher data?
why: DESE’s teacher data prints a share of teachers it calls experienced; the workbook we hold has one sheet and no data dictionary, and no document in the archive defines the threshold. A share over a threshold also cannot see teachers moving up steps once past it. — closes: DESE’s published definition of the experienced-teacher share in its teacher data file.

what: How much of each teacher’s gross pay is base salary, and how much is stipends, coaching, longevity or summer work?
why: The town’s annual reports print every town and school employee’s gross pay for the calendar year, by name, and joined to the school rosters it gives a distribution of teacher pay (see /school-spending-history/teachers-on-the-scale). But gross pay is ONE figure per person: it folds the schedule cell together with stipends, coaching, longevity, summer work and any retroactive pay, and a calendar year straddles two contract years. So a teacher paid more than a lane’s top step may be on that step, or lower in a higher lane, or lower with extra duties, and the list cannot tell which. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: where any teacher sits on the schedule. — closes: the district’s payroll earnings report for the year, by employee and earnings code (base, stipend, longevity, coaching), counts only, or the step-and-lane placement count itself.

what: Do the teachers of Ashburnham-Westminster, Tyngsborough, Hudson, Maynard, Uxbridge, Shrewsbury, Nashoba, Wachusett, Groton-Dunstable, Ayer Shirley, North Middlesex and Monty Tech sit as high on their own salary schedules as Lunenburg’s?
why: Harvard is measured (scripts/extract_peer_teacher_pay.py: its town report’s TEACHER section, on its own master’s top step, beside Lunenburg’s). Two more lists are read but cannot be placed on their own scale, because the salary schedule for the list’s year is not held: Ashburnham-Westminster’s FY2025 list (reprinted in Ashburnham’s 2025 report; the agreements held cover FY2017-FY2019 and FY2026-FY2028) and Tyngsborough’s 2022 Gross Wage Report (agreements held cover FY2019-FY2021 and FY2025-FY2027, and 2022 is the latest list the town posts); only their dollar quartiles are published. Hudson and Maynard print their school employees’ calendar-2025 pay, and Uxbridge its town and school employees’ calendar-2024 pay, by name with NO job title, so a teacher cannot be told from a custodian or a substitute. For Shrewsbury, Nashoba, Wachusett, Groton-Dunstable, Ayer Shirley, North Middlesex and Monty Tech no published list naming school employees was found in the member towns’ reports or on the districts’ sites (where each was looked for: notes/findings/WAGE-LISTS-COMPARISON-TOWNS.md). — closes: for Ashburnham-Westminster and Tyngsborough, the teachers’ agreements covering FY2025 and FY2022-FY2023; for the others, each district’s count of teachers by step and lane, or its payroll’s calendar-2025 gross earnings by employee with position title.

what: What does special education cost in Lunenburg all in, once the benefits and town-side costs of its staff are counted?
why: The school MUNIS journal holds every posting to every school account in every fund, FY2023-FY2026, and /special-education/sped-all-funds sums the accounts the ledger labels special education across the general fund, the circuit breaker and the IDEA grants. That is the most complete view the archive holds and it is still a set of postings, not a cost: health insurance and other benefits are charged to school-wide or town accounts, not to a special education line, and special education work paid from accounts with no special education label (district-wide specialists, guidance, nurses) is not separable. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: the full cost of special education in any year. — closes: the district’s End of Year Financial Report, special education program, with benefits and town-side costs allocated by program.

what: Why did the circuit breaker and the special education grants pay a smaller share of special education in FY2026 than in FY2023?
why: The school journal shows the share of special education postings outside the general fund falling over FY2023-FY2026 (/special-education/sped-all-funds), and that in FY2026 the circuit breaker fund paid through a single year-end reclassification of collaborative tuition rather than through invoices during the year. A smaller reimbursement, a balance held back for the next year, and costs moved to other accounts all fit the same postings, and nothing in a ledger says which. — closes: the district’s circuit breaker and IDEA spending plans for FY2023-FY2026, and the circuit breaker account statement for each year.

what: Which providers’ tuition did the FY2026 year-end reclassification to the circuit breaker cover?
why: In FY2026 one journal entry, `RECLASS COLLABORATIVE TUITION`, moved collaborative tuition from the general fund to the circuit breaker fund. A journal entry carries no payee, so /special-education/sped-providers attributes each provider’s invoices to the fund they were first paid from, and the FY2026 split by fund is unknowable from the ledger for whatever the entry moved. — closes: the supporting schedule for the FY2026 year-end reclassification of collaborative tuition, listing the invoices it moved.

what: What did FLLAC’s (Keystone’s) payments buy, for how many Lunenburg students, at what rates?
