why: The FLLAC Educational Collaborative runs the Keystone program (the journal’s invoice numbers on this vendor carry KEY and its descriptions read TUITION FOR KEYSTONE). It was the largest special education payee in the school journal, FY2023-FY2026, paid from tuition and contracted related-services accounts, and its payments rose far faster than special education vendor payments overall (/special-education/sped-providers). WHAT THE DOCUMENTS SAY: the Finance Committee minutes of 14 March 2024 record a discussion of Keystone’s rates being raised almost 11%, and of how a 14% increase was absorbed the year before. Keystone’s quarterly updates to the School Committee (district-budget/docs/sc-meetings/, 2023-2025) report its census for ALL member districts together, and say it grew 11% from 2021 to September 2024. A 1 June 2023 memo to Keystone’s executive board, in the School Committee packet, records the collaborative buying 143 Joslin Street, Leominster, with a $5.377 million loan, for “the collaborative’s growing need for space”; Lunenburg’s superintendent voted for it as a board member. The collaborative agreement says tuition rates are set by Keystone’s board through its budget and sent to members by 30 June. WHAT IS NOT SETTLED: none of these gives Lunenburg’s own count of students at Keystone or its own tuition, and the stated rate and census changes are far smaller than the rise in Lunenburg’s payments. Whether the rest is more Lunenburg students, more services or longer placements is not in anything held. — closes: Keystone’s count of Lunenburg students and services by year, FY2023-FY2026, with its tuition rate sheets for each year.

what: How much of the rise in school costs was higher prices, and how much was more of what the schools buy?
why: /school-spending-history/inflation-and-school-costs sets each kind of school spending, FY2009 to FY2025, against Boston-area household prices, and compares the largest recurring bills in the school MUNIS journal payment for payment, FY2023 to FY2026. Both measure dollars, not prices. A budget line is price times quantity; a matched bill holds the payee, the account and the number of payments a year constant, but not what each payment buys -- the buses run each day (the Dee Bus row), the subscribers on each health plan tier (the enrollment row), the kilowatt-hours. And household prices are not what a school pays for salaries, insurance or tuition (the constant-dollars row). So the page can say which costs grew faster than prices; it cannot say how much of any rise was price, and so cannot say how much of the school deficit -- the level-service budget less the appropriation -- rising prices produced. — closes: the district’s level-service budget worksheets for each year, with every line’s price and quantity assumptions, and the rate sheets behind each recurring bill (daily rate per bus and buses run, premium per tier and subscribers, rate per kWh), from the Business Office.

what: Were the building jobs the schools usually pay for, and the purchase orders closed unpaid, done another way in FY2026 — or not done?
why: The journal shows ten payees used every year paid under half as usual in FY2026, five of them nothing (security service, door systems, boiler inspections, piano tuning, irrigation), and $67,393 of purchase orders on contracted building services released unpaid, $37,626 of them carried in from FY2025. A payment from another account, a new vendor record, a warranty or a dropped job all look the same in a ledger. Asked by the Finance Committee for each contract and its end date, the district named five contractors and gave no dates — closes: the facilities work orders for FY2026, by building and job, and each service contract with its scope and term

what: How fast did the price of out-of-district tuition and of school bus contracts rise, year by year?
why: /school-spending-history/inflation-and-school-costs measures each kind of school spending, FY2009 to FY2025, against a published price index for that kind of thing -- school pay, public employers’ benefits, groceries, home energy -- and has none for tuition or buses. The state’s Operational Services Division sets approved special education school prices by an inflation factor each year but publishes only the current year’s estimate (mass.gov answered 404 for every earlier year asked, 20 October 2026), and the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes no price index for school bus transportation. Both are measured against household prices instead, which are not what a school pays. Every index used is national or regional, not Lunenburg’s own price, and none says how much of any rise was price rather than more placements, more buses or more staff. — closes: the Operational Services Division’s approved price for each placement Lunenburg paid, by fiscal year, and each year’s bus contract with its daily rate per bus and the number of buses, from the Business Office.

what: What exactly did the warrants of the May 2025 Annual, the November 2025 Special, the August 2016 Special and every Town Meeting from 2011 to 2014 ask, article by article, and what did the Clerk record for the 38 votes printed without a meeting date?
why: The archive holds no warrant booklet for those meetings, so their articles are known only from the Town Clerk's record in the annual report (a summary of each vote) and, from 2021, our notes of the recordings; and the FY2011-FY2013 reports print 38 votes under headings with no date. — closes: the posted warrant for each meeting, and the Clerk's dated proceedings for FY2011-FY2013.

what: Why the IDEA grant stopped being booked to the teaching and materials headings in FY2025
why: MEASURED in the school MUNIS journal (/school-all-funds/grant-coding): every IDEA entitlement grant from FY2021 to FY2024 posted its spending to function 2300 or 2400 -- headings that name teaching and instructional materials but no single voted line. The FY2025 grant posted most of its spending to 0000, no function at all, and the FY2026 grant to 2000, the instruction heading. The ledger records the change and not the reason: a new account set-up, a change of staff in the business office, or a decision to code at the grant level all fit the same postings. — closes: the business office's account set-up for each IDEA grant, FY2023-FY2026, and the IDEA budgets the district filed with DESE by function code.

what: Which voted budget line the grant and revolving spending booked to no function code served
why: MEASURED: in the school MUNIS journal most spending outside the general fund in FY2026 posts to function 0000 or to a heading (1000, 2000, 2300, 2400, 4000), not to any line the general fund budget is voted on (/school-all-funds/budget-lines-all-funds, which shows it as its own row and does not spread it). The district's End of Year Financial Report to DESE does put grant spending on function codes, so the attribution is made somewhere outside the town's ledger. This narrows `Which budget line each dollar of grant and revolving money paid for`: the ledger cannot answer it either. — closes: the district's End of Year Financial Report working papers, grant and revolving columns by function, FY2023-FY2026.

what: What the school revolving funds and the circuit breaker held at 30 June 2026
why: The FY2023 annual town report prints each school special revenue fund's balance carried; the school journal gives every receipt and payment since. /school-all-funds/unspent-by-fund rolls the first forward with the second, and that is OUR arithmetic, not a balance anybody printed: it assumes the journal holds every receipt (one fund's interest is booked outside the school department) and it does not take off orders still open. The FY2024 and FY2025 annual reports' special revenue schedules are held and not yet read. — closes: the Town Accountant's special revenue fund balances at 30 June 2024, 2025 and 2026, school funds.

what: Whether an unspent school grant budget was carried into the next grant year or simply never drawn
why: MEASURED: the grants named for FY2023 and FY2024 spent less than the budget the ledger loaded for them (/school-all-funds/unspent-by-fund). A loaded budget is not always the award -- two FY2026 funds each carry a Title I budget and one has spent nothing -- and some federal grants allow a carryover into the next year's grant, so the shortfall is not established as money lost. — closes: DESE's grant award notices, final expenditure reports and carryover approvals for each school grant, FY2023-FY2026.

what: Whether the school committee sets the special education budget expecting the circuit breaker and grants to pay the rest
why: MEASURED (/special-education/sped-all-funds): on the accounts the ledger labels special education, the general fund came in under its voted budget in three of the four years FY2023-FY2026 and ran over in FY2026 (spent counting what was still owed at year end), and the circuit breaker and grants paid more on top -- so total special education spending passed the vote every year. SETTLED FOR ONE PART: the circuit breaker on collaborative tuition. The FY2025 and FY2026 approved books print a circuit breaker offset under that line, the voted figure is the line less the offset, and the FY2025 ledger loads the line gross and cuts it by the offset on 1 July (/school-all-funds/fy-breakdown, the plan against what happened). The FY2023 and FY2024 books print no offset. STILL OPEN: no book prints any grant offset, so whether the vote counted on grants, or on the circuit breaker for any other line, is intent no document held records. — closes: the district's special education budget build for each year, with the circuit breaker and grant offsets it assumed.

what: Why the district's grant history and DESE's allocations disagree for Lunenburg's special education grants
why: MEASURED: the district's own grants history (sources/data/grants-history.csv, read from the superintendent's FY25 budget update, pp. 32-36, and the FY24 presentation, p. 16) and DESE's entitlement allocation pages (sources/data/dese-entitlement-allocations.csv, every year reconciled to DESE's by-district page) disagree for Lunenburg. IDEA 240: FY2020 $367,980 in the budget book against $369,440 at DESE; FY2024 $418,237 against $420,163; FY2021-FY2023 agree. Early childhood 262: FY2020 $12,281 vs $12,303, FY2021 $12,368 vs $12,401, FY2023 $13,133 vs $13,083, FY2024 $13,245 vs $13,325; FY2022 agrees at $12,500. ARP IDEA: the budget book lists $88,330 and $8,229 in each of FY2020, FY2021 and FY2022, and $87,888 on grant 252 in FY2023; DESE prints 252 ($88,330) and 264 ($8,229) for FY2022 only. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: why. An allocation DESE revised after the book was printed, the book reporting a different stage (a budgeted or amended award, a carryover, a draw) under the same name, or a multi-year grant printed in each year it was spent all fit; nothing here tests any of them, and no earlier version of these pages is held here -- our weekly snapshots begin 23 October 2026. FY2018 IDEA cannot be checked across views: DESE's by-fund-code page for 0240 FY2018 answers with its server error page. -- closes: the grant award letters (DESE's GEM$ project award and any amendments) for funds 240, 262, 252 and 264, FY2020-FY2024, which state the amount awarded and its period.

what: Why Lunenburg's IDEA special education allocation per pupil is lower than most comparable districts'
why: MEASURED (/school-all-funds/grant-allocations-compared): DESE's IDEA allocation divided by DESE's October headcount puts Lunenburg below the median of its comparison districts in every year that can be compared since FY2017. NOT ESTABLISHED: why. DESE's eligibility text names enrolment in public and private schools and children in poverty as inputs; our divisor counts only pupils enrolled in the district, and the formula's other parts are not on DESE's allocation pages. A smaller resident count, a smaller poverty count or a historical base amount all fit. — closes: DESE's IDEA Part B allocation calculation for Lunenburg, FY2017-FY2027, showing each input.

what: Whether Lunenburg receives Title III English-learner money through a consortium
why: MEASURED (/school-all-funds/grants-others-receive): most of Lunenburg's comparison districts are allocated Title III; Lunenburg is on none of DESE's Title III allocation pages, FY2017-FY2027. DESE allocates Title III only where a district's amount reaches the statutory floor, and at the median rate per learner our estimate puts Lunenburg just under it. A district under the floor can join a consortium, and DESE's pages do not list a consortium's members. — closes: DESE's Title III consortium membership list for each year, or the district's Title III application.

what: Which competitive state and federal grants the school district applied for and won, by year
why: DESE's allocation pages list formula entitlements only, and its open-grants list shows what is open now, not who was awarded. So the grant comparison (/school-all-funds/grants-others-receive) cannot compare what Lunenburg applied for or won against other districts. — closes: the district's grants list by year, with the application and award notice for each competitive grant, and DESE's award listings for the same years.

what: Whether a year's special education overrun on the general fund measures surprise, or how much was charged to the circuit breaker account at the close
why: MEASURED (/special-education/special-education-overruns): the need a Special Education Reserve Fund is sized against is the general fund's spending past its vote, line by line, after the circuit breaker account (fund 2640) and the grants paid their share. The circuit breaker account paid tuition in every year FY2023-FY2026, and in FY2026 it paid through a single year-end reclassification of collaborative tuition rather than through invoices during the year (/special-education/sped-all-funds). So how much of a year's tuition lands on the general fund, and therefore that year's overrun, turns partly on a charge decided at the close. Set the account's tuition back on the line and FY2024's need is $619,020 rather than $152,724. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the amount charged each year follows a rule (the reimbursement received, a planned share, whatever kept the general fund within its vote), so the year-to-year spread of the general fund need cannot be separated from the spread of that choice. — closes: the district's circuit breaker spending plan for each year, set before the year began, against which the year-end charge can be compared.

what: Whether the Special Education Reserve Fund may be drawn while other special education lines are under their votes
why: MEASURED (/special-education/special-education-overruns): over FY2010-FY2026 at least one of the three special education lines (in district, out-of-district tuition, transportation) ran over its vote in 12 years, but the three together ran over in only 6 -- so in 6 years an overrun on one line sat inside a special education total that came in under. Whether the reserve pays a line's overrun in such a year, or only once money has been moved between lines, decides which series it should be sized against, and the page sizes it on the first, which is OUR choice. The Town Manager's description at the Select Board (7 October 2025) gives the vote needed to spend from the fund and its cap, not the order of draws. A Special Education Reserve Fund Policy is on the Select Board agenda for 27 October 2026. — closes: the Special Education Reserve Fund policy as adopted by the Select Board and the School Committee.

what: Which ledger accounts and budget lines make up the special education share DESE reports for a mixed function?
why: MEASURED (sources/data/sped-crosswalk.csv, /special-education/sped-definition): DESE counts special education as a PROGRAM inside a function, and the district's FY2023 and FY2024 End of Year Report working copies put part of supervision (2110), classroom teaching (2305), substitutes (2324, 2325), paraprofessionals (2330), guidance (2710) and psychology (2800) in the Special Education column. The report prints one figure per function and program; the Town's ledger and the district's budget book can be read account by account and line by line, and no document held says which accounts or lines make up each share. So the difference between DESE's total and each of our three definitions can be measured by function and cannot be traced to accounts. — closes: the district's worksheet mapping each MUNIS account to an End of Year Report line and program, FY2023 and FY2024.

what: Under which DESE function does the district report its own function codes 2310, 2315, 2357 and 2900?
why: The Town's account strings and the district's budget book use function codes 2310 (special education teachers, tutoring and contracted services), 2315, 2357 and 2900 (social workers), none of which is in DESE's FY2025 chart of accounts (dese-eoyr-fy2025-function-crosswalk.xlsx, sheet codes), and the FY2023 and FY2024 End of Year Report working copies print no line for them. The crosswalk compares them within their DESE group by first two digits, which is our grouping, not a published mapping. — closes: the district's worksheet mapping each MUNIS account to an End of Year Report line and program, FY2023 and FY2024.

what: Why a school purchase order was still open on 30 June, and why an order carried into the next year was closed with nothing paid
why: MEASURED (/school-all-funds/carried-over-orders): at each close the school journal zeroes every open order (YEC) and reopens it on 1 July (SOY), and a carry-forward transfer raises the next year's budget by the same amount; of the general fund orders carried out of FY2023-FY2025, 68% were paid the next year and the rest closed with nothing paid against them. Neither the journal nor the period-13 reports say why an order was open at the year end (goods not delivered, an invoice not received, a deliberate hold of budget), or why a carried order was closed rather than paid, or whether what it was for was bought again on a new order (one revolving-fund order, Nature's Classroom, was closed and the same amount paid on a new one). So the size of the carry is measured and its cause is not. — closes: the district’s year-end list of open purchase orders, with the reason each was kept open or closed, FY2023-FY2026.

what: Why the FY2023 annual town report and the school journal disagree, fund by fund, on special education grant spending
why: MEASURED (/special-education/special-education-overruns, the ten-year table): for FY2023 the annual town report's Special Revenue Funds schedule prints disbursements of $562,063.28 from the special education grant funds and the school journal posts $560,954.43 to the same grants (payments plus what was still owed) -- $1,108.85 apart in total, while the circuit breaker account (fund 2640) agrees to the cent, $494,967.72. Fund by fund the gap is larger and runs both ways: the FY2022 #240 grant is $10,495.25 higher in the journal, the FY2023 #240 grant $3,564.68 higher, the FY2021 #240 grant $670.67 lower, and the report prints two #262 rows ($12,500.00 and $1,998.11) the journal has no FY2023 postings for. The page uses the report's disbursements for FY2017-FY2022, where no journal is held. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the difference is timing (cash paid against obligations recorded), grant-year attribution, or a transcription in one of the two. -- closes: the Town Accountant's FY2023 trial balance for the school grant funds, showing expenditures and encumbrances by fund.

what: What did Town Meeting vote before May 2011?
why: The archive's record of Town Meeting votes is the Town Clerk's printed proceedings in the annual town reports, and the earliest report it holds is FY2011, so /town-meeting-votes begins with the 7 May 2011 Annual Town Meeting. Nothing earlier is missing from the page by choice; it is not in the archive. — closes: the annual town reports for FY2010 and earlier, or the Town Clerk's certified record of each earlier Town Meeting.

what: What did the Town Clerk record for the 2026 Town Meetings, and for the warrant articles the extracted Clerk's record does not reach?
why: Results for the May and September 2026 meetings come only from our reading of the meeting videos, because the annual town report that prints the Clerk's record of them is not yet in the archive. For FY2015 onward the Clerk's record as extracted (town-meeting-votes.csv) also does not reach every article on the posted warrant; /town-meeting-votes counts the shortfall year by year. Either the Clerk's pages print fewer articles or our extraction missed them, and nothing here yet tells which. — closes: the FY2026 annual town report's Town Clerk section, and a page-by-page re-read of the Clerk's proceedings in the FY2015-FY2025 reports.

what: Which competitive DESE grants Lunenburg applied for and did not win
why: DESE's award documents name only the districts that won. Comparison districts won competitive grants in FY2026 and FY2027 that Lunenburg did not (/school-all-funds/grants-others-receive), and nothing published says whether the district applied for them. — closes: the district's list of the DESE grant applications it submitted, by year, with each outcome

what: DESE's competitive award lists before FY2026
why: DESE's Grant Allocations & Awards page links competitive award lists for FY2026 and the current year only; fy25-awards.html, fy24- and fy23- redirect to its 404 page (checked 23 October 2026). So who won a competitive grant before FY2026 cannot be compared. — closes: DESE's competitive award lists for FY2023 to FY2025, by records request

what: How much of the federal grant money Monty Tech is allocated serves Lunenburg students
why: DESE allocates Perkins, IDEA and the Title grants to Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical as one district, and it serves students from every member town (/school-all-funds/grants-others-receive). Lunenburg gets no Perkins allocation of its own, and nothing published says what part of Monty Tech's serves Lunenburg's students. — closes: Monty Tech's grant applications and budgets, by programme and by member town

what: What Monty Tech’s tuition, payments from other school systems and miscellaneous local revenue were for
why: The Census Bureau’s FY2024 school finance survey reports three large local items for Monty Tech that are neither its member towns’ assessments nor private gifts: tuition from pupils, parents and private sources (item A07), payments from other school systems for tuition, transportation and other services (D11), and refunds and other local revenue (U97). The amounts are on /monty-tech/monty-tech-revenue, item by item. The survey names each item and says nothing about what produced it. Monty Tech’s FY2024 budget book lists Practical Nursing and Continuing and Post Graduate Studies staff among those paid from revolving or special-revenue funds, so programmes that could charge tuition exist; it prints no revenue for them, and its general-fund revenue table budgets nothing for miscellaneous receipts or interest. So whether A07 is adult and practical-nursing tuition, whether D11 is tuition for out-of-district pupils, and what U97 holds are hypotheses nothing here tests. — closes: Monty Tech’s audited financial statements for FY2024, which report revenue by fund, and its revenue detail by account for the same year.

what: Which of the district's psychologists and adjustment counselors does it report to the state as special education staff?
why: MEASURED (sources/data/sped-definition.csv, /special-education/sped-definition): DESE counts a school psychologist or adjustment counselor as special education only under the special education job code (EPIMS 3361 and 3351, against 3360 and 3350; EOYR-EPIMS crosswalk in DESE's FY2025 printing version, rows 84 to 88). The Town's ledger carries accounts, not job codes, and the district's two End of Year Report working copies disagree: FY2023 puts every psychologist account in special education, FY2024 puts the same accounts in regular day. So psychology and guidance are left out of every special education total on this site, and the part DESE counts cannot be traced to people or accounts. — closes: the district's EPIMS staff records by job classification for its psychologists, adjustment counselors and social workers, FY2023 and FY2024.

what: Why does the FY2024 End of Year Report working copy repeat FY2023's special education figures for guidance, psychology and two substitute lines?
why: MEASURED (sources/data/sped-definition.csv, checked by scripts/build_sped_crosswalk.py): five Special Education cells of the FY2024 working copy (eoy24!F173, F178, F258, F262 and F274) equal the FY2023 copy's to the dollar, and the psychology figure matches no FY2024 ledger account while the FY2024 psychologist salaries sit, whole, in the Regular Day column. Whether the five were carried forward unchanged, or the report as filed differs, is not stated in the working copy. — closes: the FY2024 End of Year Financial Report as filed with DESE.

what: Why a special education line ran over its vote in a given year: a new child, a higher tuition rate, or a longer route?
why: MEASURED (/special-education-reserve/surprise-costs): over FY2010-FY2026 out-of-district tuition was the largest share of every dollar the three special education lines ran over their votes, transportation next, in-district services last. The ledger records the overrun and not its cause; the district's own deck to the Finance Committee (22 October 2026, slide 9) names all three -- new student needs, tuition increases, transportation changes -- and every one lands as the same figure on the line. A reserve sized on the total cannot say which risk it is carrying. — closes: the district's year-end explanation of each special education line's variance, by cause.

what: Which posts each grant and fee fund pays for, and how much of each post
why: The school journal posts payroll one line per account per pay run and records no person, and grant pay posts to accounts named for a kind of work (support salaries, instructional salaries), so a grant can be totalled but not tied to a post. Year-end entries also move pay between funds, mostly citing school memos not in this archive (/school-all-funds/pay-moved-between-funds). — closes: the Town’s MUNIS payroll distribution report, each employee’s pay by fund and account, FY2023–FY2026; or the district’s grant budgets filed with DESE, which list the posts each grant pays.

what: What does a child arriving with an education plan cost Lunenburg's own schools, when the plan needs staff the budget did not carry?

what: Why did the federal special education grant pay a private placement in FY2026 that the general fund paid in FY2025, and did the FY2026 budget expect it?
